The incident referred to by Mr. Geoghegan at the conclusion of his brilliant address to the jury in the Neill case of having seen many Years ago for tit e first time sentence of death passed occurred bo lal back as October, 1877. It was a case in which an imbecile had been deliberately starved to death. It was known popularly as the 'Penge Mystery," and crested a great sensation at the time.

The Duke of Hozburghe was a noted sportsman 'Wilk; day. He played for many seasons with thel tflexburghshire cricket team, and could handle a salmon rod as wtll as most people. Floors Castle, ?the chief residence of the family, is a magnificent wide near Kelso, built about two centuries ago on the site of an older castle ‘which was peculiarly 1 rich in historical associations. It was at the famous siege of this castle that James H. of Scot- land was killed.

Some of the loveliest,retsches of the Tweed are ' through and round the park at Floors, affording salmon fishing unsurpassed in this part of Scotland. The late Duke never ecluslled the achievement of his father, who in one day, about twenty years ago, landed with his own rod twenty-seven salmon and grilse. This portion of the Tweed is the dividing line between England and SBothind. The Rox- burgh estates extend to about sixty thousand acres, and have 6 rental '-value of about .£50,000 a year. Sir Charles LiHey, whose resigeAction of the post of Chief Justice of Queensland is Lunounced, has long been one of the most prominent •figures in Australian legal circle.. His careerot the Colonial Bar was one of plienomenstrapidity. e look silk four years aftet Commencing to plead, and, embark- ing on politics, became successively Attorney- General, Colonial Secretary, and Premier of the ' Colony. Twelve years ago he was appoiteted Chief , Justice. Sir Charles holds strong views en the sub- ject of Colonial independence, and expresses them, with the utmost frankness. His most notable acti was the founding of free education in Queensland in 1870. He Wil3 at one time editor and part owner of the "Brisbane Courier." His salary as Chief! Justice was £2,500 a year, a thousand less than is received by the judicial heads of Victoria and New; South Wales.

I Rev. Richard F. Clarke, whose assault on thr i!teaohing and character of Theosophy put Mrs. Bet and Mr. Burrows an the defensive on Taw- day might at St. James's Hall, is a well-known • jesuit. He was formerly sttachell to the church in Farm-st., and has lately been in Thildin and Man- chester. He is editor of the " Month " magazine, in which his article againq the new creed appeared When at Oxford about thirty years ago, there were few students who would care to encounter "'Clarke of John's." 80 brilliant were hi achievements in the scholastic arena. As a preachert lie attracts large audiences in the Jesuit churches of London, Dublin and Manchester, which are generally the , fields of his labour every alternate year. His published writings are mostly devoted to Catholic philosophy.

It is news that the Empress of German is ex- travagant. Yet tile "World ' save that she iz, and declares that she never will appear in public a second time in a toilette,and that she always wears materials of the very best. The experience of those who have often seen her seem to tall foul of this statement. Richly dressed perhaps she is, but so very quietly and unobtrusively, and with NO little individuality of style, that it would be difficult to detect whether her cobteme was one that had been seen before ornot. Her childhood was spent in real poverty, at any rate in tn poverty of a German princeling' s court, which can be very poor, as the I testimony of our oirn Plinceis Alice of Hesse, who often had a difficulty in finding money for new curtains, has proved to US. -The German Empress an a girl was obliged to be very modest in her de- mands, just as the Princess of Wales was. And just as our Princess does not disdain to wear a gown ti at suits her over and over again at public func- tions, so surely is the German Empress sensible in like manner.

CHAPTER XXIV. JEALOUSY, THE CRUELEST OF ALL PANGS TO EN- DURE. THROBBED IN HER HEART. Was it only her fancy ?" she wondered, "or did a startled cry break from Arthur Rochester's lips?" "It is not to be thought of, Elaine," le said, hurriedly and hoarsely. "I hope you will gbandon the idea."

"Do you not like Miss Lawrence ?" she asked. wonderingly. "She is very beautiful, and destined to be very popular." "That will be nothing to me," he responded, desperately. "How strange that you should have taken such a dislike to her I" said Elaine. "Most gentlemen admire her."
"We will not talk about her," he said, with forced calmness.

But Elaine had no intention of giving up the, subject so easily. "I have a Paint recollection of having seen her before somewhere," she went on, "even her name sounds slightly familiar. "Do you know, Arthur, I felt just just a little jealous. I thought you were ' watching her all the evening, and for a time I—yes, I might as well confess it—l felt miserable. You , will never give me cause for jealousy, will you, Arthur 2" she added, quickly; "I came of a race to whom jealousy was fatal." "You need have no fear, Elaine. I will never give you cause for one unhappy moment," he an I ewered, gently. During the fortnight. that followed, Arthur did his best to control the unhappy, despondent state Into which he was slowly but surely drifting. He was Elaine's betrothed husband, but he was by no means her lover. He tried his best to be all that was kind and considerate to her, but he never dreamed of giving her one single caress which is so dear to girlish hearts from the one they love. He was quick at reading women's faces, and he knew by the wistful expression of Elaine's that she expected some demonstration of Jove from him ; and he .often took her hand, speaking some kindly word of praise that made the girl's heart beat and her cheeks glow—that was in place.of the kiss Lie.sheuld have given her and could not. Yet Fakm with Elaine's happy voice ringing in his ears, with her bright, laughing face before him, with all the knowledge of the intensity of happiness his love had brought her, there were times when his heart rnisgave him, and did not see how he was to endure it. There were times when he would have given his life almost to have freed himself from the engage- ment he had made on the impulse of the moment. There were times when, in his desperation, he thought it wculd be easier to die than to call any other girl save lonic his wife; when he would have gone away, never to return. But one thought re- strained him, and that thought was that Elaine's heart would surely break. Ah, no 1 no one must suffer for him, he resolved, what he had suffered for the one whom he had ' loved and lost. There was a grim satisfaction for him in the knowledge that, seeing him with Elaine, bole would not think that the treachery had broken his heart. It was quite a puzzle to Elaine why Arthur seemed to take sueh a determined dislike to beautiful lonie, Colonel Whitney's niece. He had'but to hear that she was to be at a plaoe to refuse absolutely to go there. "How strarga that you have taken such an aver- sion to the gin, and without any reason 1" laughed Elaine, "Talk aboat the prejudice of ladies, it is nothing compared to the prejudice of gentlemen. When they make their mind up against a person they cannot be induced to re-consider their opinion." An event happened a week later, however, which was a keen blow to Elaine's peace of mind, that aroused all the latent jealousy in her nature, which lay like a smouldering volcano beneath a calm surface. It came about in this way.: To some worthy poor man employed in the mill, Miss Rochester had promised a supply of cast-off clothing. In search- ing through Arthur's wardrobe, having called Elaine to assist her, she came across a velvet shoot- , lug-jacket which she remembered to have heard Arthur say he should never wear again. "This will answer quite well," she said, handing I It to Elaine, adding: "Please take it down to the i man, my dear.; he is below in the servants' hall. Bay that I shall find more for him in the course of a few days, when I shall have more time." As Elaine reached the lower corridor a sudden Impulse caused her to thrust her hand in the pockets, to make sure they were empty. In the last one she found a scrap of paper. Drawing it .forth, she looked at it, carelessly enough. Then, in one short instant, the ,colour died from her face, the light from her eyes. She gave a quick gasp, sinking down on the nearest seat. "Let me read it again," she cried, hoarsely, "to make sure that there is no mistake—that my eyes have not deceived me." It was but a scrap of a letter written in a fine,' pretty, delicate hand, and read as follows: lligginning to believe you every foolishly, exacting lover. You should know very well, dear, that your lonie does love you, even though I fail to ; write it in each letter. You have only been gone three days, Arthur, yet I count the hours until you ,return. In the language of the poet I say; 'I never knew how dear thou wert to me, until you went away.' I shall not—" The fragment contained but those few words, but they were a terrible revelation to the girl who read them. Her eyes were flaming, her hands clenched, her heart beating with quick, convulsive sobs. She read the words over and over again, and each time they seemed like so many dagger-thrusts in her breast. She forgot her errand. For two Jong hours she sat there, but they seemed like so many moments. Who was this girl who dared write to Arthur in 'this fashion? They must have been lovers I and a :spasm of pain shot through her heart at the very , thought. Thole 1 The name was an uncommon .one. She repeated it over and over again. Snd- .denly a thought came to her. She remembered how _

as the carriage rollel along. Her heart was bitter with tutuultuous thoughts. 1. shall soon find out if it is she whom he loved. If it is, I shall hate her with a hatred more bitter than death. I shall not accept half a heart. I 'want a whole heart or none. If !he has ever loved ' Arthur Rochester I shall be her bitterest foe. Lave cannot die easily out of the human heart. If they have loved each otLer once, that love has never 'wholly died out." Let those who read of the tragedy that followed remember how different poor, wilful, misguided Elaine's life had been to that of other girls. Her mother lad died in her infancy; she had grown up without 11. mother's guidance, without a sister's• kindly admonition. Her own will was her law. No one had counselled her against.the bitter fires of jealousy, the sinfalneEs of hatred and thirst for revenge. It was quite a surprise to Tonle when, half an hour later, Elaine's card was brought up to her. "Why does this girl thrust her friendship on me 7" se sobbed. "It will be a cruel torture for me to smile kindly into the face of the girl Arthur Rochester loves—the girl whom he is to make his bride." For a moment bitter sobs shook her frame • then she rose calmly, and dried her eyes. The call that followed the tempest had come.
'• I must not rail at Heaven for taking him from me and giving him to her," she murmured, "since It was God's will." _

.„ Her step faltered slightly,. and the slender figure trembled as she walked slowly down the corridor and entered the drawing-room, "Miss Granger," she said, huskily, extending her hand. Elaine took it, and they stood for a moment gazing steadily into each other's eyes—lonie and the girl who was destined to be her bitterest foe— end all for love's sake—love for the same man.

CHAPTER XXV. "I GANT, THE DEEP LOVE OF MY HEART TO OFE WED WAS FALSE AS SHE WAS FAIR." "This . is quite an unexpected pleasure, Miss Granger," said Joule, constrainedly, as she teok a seat opnositelhe visitor. "I have thought of little else save yourself ever since we met at the ball," returned Elaine, "and I took the opportunity of calling as soon as possible. Do you know,' she went on, lightly, "your face actually haunts me? I cannot shake off the im- pression that we have met before." As she spoke she looked keenly into the lovely, fifice opposite her. She expected a reply, but lonie vouchsafed. none. After a few moments of indifferent con; versation, Elaine turned suddenly to lonie with the query: "Did you know Mr. Rochester before the evening of the ball, Miss Lawrence?" She saw the lovely face flash, then pale; then lonia lifted her dark eyes, and frankly answered: "Yes." How Elaine longed to ask the question that fairly burned her lips: If she was the lonic: Arthur Rochester had loved? But there was a certain dignity about her that forbade questioning. "The name is uncommon," she remarked. "I do not know that I have ever heard it before. I had almost forgotten the real object of my visit, Miss Lawrence,' she said, laughingly, "I am thinking of getting up a garden party in your honour, if you—" The sentence was never finished. A gasping cry fell from lonie's lips. She drew her chair closer to Elaine's and took her hands impulsively in her own. "Do not think me rude," she said, hastily, "but hope you will abandon the idea." "You must have a reason for declining, and a very strong one," said Elaine. "Would you mind . telling me why you do not care for 'I?" lonic's lips quivered. How could she say that it would be but a cruel torture to her to cross Arthur Rochester's threshold—to look upon his face again —to hear him speak tender words, just as he used to speak to her, to this girl who was soon to be his wife, if report spoke truly. "Because I care so little for social gatherings," replied lonie, hesitatingly. "My uncle, Colonel, . Whitney, is far from well. On the night I returned from the ball I found him in a deep swoon in his chair. I have determined to remain at home for • the present and minister to his comfort." "It is a wonder that Mr. Lyons, your betrothed, will consent to any such arrangement," smiled Elaine; seeing a chance to score a hit then and there by adding: He must be very different from my—my—lover. Arthur often says to me, Enjoy your single blessedness as much as you will, Elaine, my darling, for soon you will belong to me, and I am going to be selfish enough to be jealous then of every moment spent away from me.'" She saw the face into which she gazed grow very white, as though it was an effort to listen with cal m. mess. "Do you know," said Elaine, meditatively, "al- though I have many girl friends, I have not one confidante among them, and I should like one so much. How I should like to make one of you, Miss Lawrence—lonie I But somehow I have con- ceived the idea that you don't quite like me. I cannot tell why." "Why should I not like you, Miss Granger ?" said lonie, confusedly. "As for friendships, lam slow to make them." "For that reason I should prize yours all the more," declared Elaine. "I should like to tell you my hopes and pretty day-dreams—how happy I am." " Oh l if she knew that every word stabbed my heart she would not utter them," thought Joule. "I will never, no, never be the confidante of the girl whom Arthur Rochester now loves." "You are very good to repose so mu.-.. 11 confi- dence in me," saki. lonic, adding, with an effort: "Have you ever spoke to Mr.—Mr.—Rochester of me ?" "Certainly," replied Elaine. "And when I told him I should like you for my best and dearest friend, he laughed as though the idea was vastly aren:ing to him. Gentlemen do not understand, you see, bow much young girls love confidantes." "Well," said Elaine at length, rising to depart, "if you won't permit me to give a garden party in your honour, yon must at least accept my invitation to luncheon to-morrow. Now do not find an excuse to avoid that." "I cannot promise just now," returned lonie, evasively. "If I can come, I will .rop you a note to that effect." Elaine's eyes glowed restlessly. This was what she desired above all things. Then she would know beyond a doubt if the scrap of paper she had found in the pocket of the shooting jacket was in lonie Lawrence's handwriting. -
Arthur appeared to dislike Miss Lawrence, Colonel Whitney's niece. Was it because her name was lonie, too?.
All night long Elaine tossed restlessly upon her pillow pondering over the matter. The note from lonie came with the early morning

[WITHOUT THH MASSINHTTIt.I -• • .JOHN PHISRS. • r (Cantina:ed.) "Good morning" said the genial Rotundity' "Have you used —." "lisTo more o' that Hai, an. -thou lovest me 1""" If it be an' add,' it is useless; if it be not, it is an impertinence. Let it suffice to say that I have used the beet soap, and as every mane- lecturer of the saponaeeous compound. and every user thereof, avers &is particular tiaponillcationt to be the best, so every one of themis herein advertis- ed (N.B. Cheques -(crossed) may be transmitted ' through the Editme. During breuktase, when I could get a word in edgeways, my host enjoinednae very strictly to see the Clipfton 'Suspension Bridge before I left town. Mist is—to see it from the top and to walk overit—having, ef course, seen it from the under-side inroming. Now the geniality was not alone in .this recommendation—on every hand "the bridge" was mentioned as Me sight of Bristol —to go away without seeing which would amount, in heinousness, to little less than sacrilege, and to be paralleled .only 'in culpability by the Mahommo- den who, being an the vicinity of Mecca, fake to visit the holy place, or say, a visitor to Warrington who neglected torinspect the Eau de Cologne works at Longford, under Aldermanic cicerone-age! And here I had wasted half a century and left this—not the Diggleedamned Attar-works, but the bridge— unvisited and unseen! True, could not very well see the bridge before it was built, but when I reflect upon the uurabeeof subsequent annual opportuni- ties thus neglected and unimproved, I am con- science-stricken. Now, remorse ie of little spiritual benefit, uniese accempanied by a well grounded,and well kept determination to reform: At whatever. pereoual sacrifice it may cost, I will see "The Bridget' And afters.: ire there no other towns in England, nay in the British Isles, with their locally indicated " lion, " thus by my remissness " left blooming alone r Alasl the map is dotted over with them as it might be from a pepper-box r But there twill reform, and the Beauties of England, and Wales, now mutely reproachful, shall no longer have !hie neglect to impute to me. I will " tour " around. But how ? Shall I start at home and be personally conducted over our own "lion "—the place of mysterious mechanism and olfactory delectation No! The subtle flavour finds us* afar off, and "proximity ioannoying." How, then? shall I hire a musical mangle and deliver "notes "as well as I take them, tramp the country and give out my crotchets at every rest; grind Beethoven and music by Handel to an appreciative audience of unsoph- isticated urchins dancing Da Capo on the pavement —a sincere but unconscious "Encore "? A cara- van ? as was once suggested and agreed upon while sitting on a rail, with a few congenial spirits, now alas tin the spirit world, assisting at the obsequies of a glorious summer sun whose lingering rays bathed the-VOrld in rosy tints, and imbued our imaginations with like hues? Yes I We resolved unanimously that it was the first and bounden duty 1 of all touriste to do" their own county first and then, if there is time, and they can, to "do" the foreigner afterwards. (N.B. Some people reverse this process by." doing " as many of their country- men eelhey can, and taking the proceeds on the continent to Awe" done brown" by the foreignei !) So we decided that for the nonce and the while it wo4ld be well to abandon respectability—" bidl'd shirts and plug 'hats "—assume a nomadic and gipsy , life—meet nature more nearly face to face and ex- plore the nooks-and corners of rural life. But alas I the wood is net groWn, or the acorn sown of which that caravan isto be made, while the iron and the project alike is—ore ! But now a brilliant and fast-ascending sun warned me to be .off and do my devoir at The Bridge." So after 'valediction, in which, of course, the sleek and he-ribboned "Sammy " was included, I sought by devious and steep-ascending ways, this shrine of Bristol pilgrims. And truly it is tl notice- able and very pleasing sight spanning the steep- sided rocky gorge-through which flews the Avon on its canal-like course to the sea. But as lam not writing a guide book—have none handy to copy from—as the Bridge.will most likely De there next year.—as ticket"; are cheap and Cook is willing-1 don't wish to bore those who lame seen it with as good or more appreeiative eyes than myself—as to those who have se seen it let me reverse Punch's advice to those about to marry." Do." As I have hinted, the Avon here is little more than a natural tidal Ship Canal. It not, I think, in some places as wide as our local effort in that direction. But the new bridge had for me less attraction than had the old river with its old associations—its old time 1 westward bound caravels of a size scarce exceed- ing a madern yate—tinycockle-shells,but manfully manned by men who sought the regions of the sett- ing sun in tubby ships no bigger than a barge. But times and manners and .ships change, and I mest, hasten over the bridge down the meandering declivitous road to the river—across the ferry,a beat rowed by a man forward. who* pushed instead of pulling his sculls, along-the bank of the river to the wharf where the " Marchioness "'was taking in last consignments of cargo ,and passengers for South Wales. This completed, we retraced our course down river, round the Arpleyelike bend which sud- denly gives place to the ,c.anon-like gorge of the precipitous carboniferous 'limestone of Clifton. Those much tilted rocks ere highly-picturesque, and are interesting geologically. andi ooald have enjoy- ed a scramble among them much, had time per- mitted. I was particularly etruckby the appearance of one ledge where the sus-face of the _stratum was hare and smooth for some twenty feet and about half that width--with an angular inclination of some 45 degrees. An awful *dace ,to got upon by accident—with the almost eertainprospeet of being ' shot.a mere hag of bones, into ;the river below. Again the Avol; lost its precipitous sides, became , marsh-bounded, and joined its little-tide with the more majestic Severn. _

Of, this placid and uneventful voyage have littleto relate". The weather was beautiffilly flne, and, its the children sing:—" All was •calm and bright." An outward-bound ocean-goer we passed just 88 she was casting off the little fussy,,puifing, tugc that had been of such essential service to her in threading the devious "-deeps -and avoiding the treacherous shallows of the winding "Lyon. I said we passed her. This is true, but sne scion reversed this state of affairs when she got more water under 1 , her,.and her" clogs to th' swing." Then she gradu- ally forged ahead, and soon we had only the tomb- stone view of her :—" Though lost to sight to memory dear." Thus she took the coneeit out of taci. Aetene collier (light) cleared out from Bristol sometime before us, and now, when we enter the Severn, we see her in tbe distance, like a smoke- emitting plank, rolling ungainly upon the water. The" Slarchieness " somewhat recovered her im- paired self-respect, by showing she had " the heels " of this wczter tumbril. On the water no one liLes taking Sir VT atki n'e place. "Driving " and "carrying on "is sometimes a necessity and some- times a pleasure but the " driving " must he of your own ship, and not some other fellow's before you! Once more in Cardiff. Once more we climb the dirty, coaly, barrel-encumbered gangway, and again tramp the long length of straight street from the docics to the town. And again I marvelled at the numerous Greek shop signs in the Greek charac- ters. That character—that alpha-beta—in which ' the grand philosophy and the cultured thought of Greece is preserved. And, strange irony of fate ! in the same character, in the same book we find at once certain theological tenets and their denuncia- Ition of this philosophy as " foolishness !" Being hungry and tired, I have no time or inclination to discuss with you, my dear reader, the question as to whether the wisdom of the Greek or the "foolish- ness" of the sect will best atand the abrading influences of time, or which it is, or whether it is, that one is crumbling to pieces beneath the wither- ing effect of the other. These, would indeed, be poor times, if one man could not think as he liked and let another believe as lie liked! Aye, even to the extent of believing that twice two were five, or that two intersecting lines were not, in their angles, invariably the complement of a circle! But, while thus aftwing anyone to believe this, without throw- ing "Cocker" or "Euclid" at his head, I should

It the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, :before Mr. F. Menke (chairman), and Aldermen.Batton, Harrison, Francomb, and Wright, Thomas Walsh, landlord of the Crown and Sceptre Inn,'Butterniarket-stewas Charged with permitting drunkenness on his ptemises, on the evening of the 18th af dnetober.—Mr: Swift, • barrister, Manches- ter and St. Ileleps, instructed by Air. Browne, appeared for the defence. P.C. ,Delahaye said about .a •quatter-past six he and P.C. Barnett were on duty opposite the defendant's house and saw three mere Patrick Garry, of 12, Dolman's-lane, and two others. Thomas Hannan and John Caren, who were assistiug biro, he being drunk, go into the Crown and Sceptre. Witness and Barnett went across and sat* Garry dreeking out of a pint jug. He entered and asked the barmaid, who was in charge, if she was aware he was drunk, and she said she was not, and Mr. Walsh was not at home. When Garry had emptied the jug, he wanted more, but she refused him, arid he was taken borne by the two other men, who lodged with him. A few minutes after, Inspector Bowen arrived, and they went to see Garry at his lodg- ings arid found him helplessly drunk in bed. In reply to Mr. Swift, the witness said Mrs. McAllister the landlady of the men was not having a glass of whisky in rite inn when they were there.—Mr. Swift asked Delakeye if it was not true that five officers namely two inspectors, a sergeamt, and two constables went to Garry's lodgings, which questions the witness did not a riswer,ibut finally said that three officers went into carry's bedroom by levitation of the landlady.— Mr. Swift What right had you to do that ? Was there a charge of felony P—The witness did not answer.— Alderman Sutton thought it was an extraordinary proceeding too into the man's bedroone—Mr. Swift again asked the witness what right he had to do it, but j received no repirr,--In further cross-examination, the j witness said Inapector Sinks had suggested that they should go to the lodgings to identify Garry. Witness was the constable in the case against Mr. Pilling, the publican, which was dismissed.—P.C. Barnett gave evi- dence corroboratiee of Dela haye's.—lnspector Bowen said the barmaid told him the men had coins in and had three pints of beer, and she did not know they were I drunk till the constable called attention to them. They ascertained at the lodgings that Garry was druuk.—Ald. Sutton: Is it usual to.go up to the houns and into a bed- 1 room in a case of this sett ?—The witness replied that it was usual where a man was a stranger, te• make sure of his address. Mr, Swift said the landlady had no right to invite the officers into the man's bedroom.. A man's bedroom was his castle. Witness, in answer to Mr. Swift, said the landlord of the ion did his best to manage his house well. He said his wife had been out on business, Witness did not suppose the affair would have happened had Mr. Walsh hism in. There-had been a wedding at the lodging-house, and they had been having drink there. —The Chairman thought eiarry probably got drunk before he went to the iute—ele. Swift said the Chairman was not justified M. drawing -that inference.—lnspector Bowen, in answer to the Beach, said he was a sworn lodging-house inspector and hada right to visit the house. I —The Chairman : That proves they have not exceeded their right.—Mr. Swift said they did not go in this case to inspect.—Alderman Sutton They went for a special object.—Mr. Swift : Certakily.—Mr. Swift argued that supposing Garry was drunk there was no permitting ' drunkenness because the drunkennesellid not take place at the inn.—The magistrates' clerk said to supply drink to one already drunk was permitting drunkenness. —Mr. Swift proceeded to deny that there was any drunkenness, or any drink ordered by the three men exer4pt a glass of whisky for their landlady, Mrs. McAllister. The three men had been in sober on the previous occasion during the afternoon; and had had three pints of beer, and it was that oceasien to which the barmaid referred, not to the tbne when the constable found them there, when she told the co:est:die that she had served them with three pints. —lf Garry ! was drinking out of a jug on the latter occasion tie hail probably picked it up off the ceunter.—liellen McAllister I deposed to being treated by the three Men to a glass of' whisky at the time in question, and to the men having nothing. She also gave evidence as to the men having some beer after they got home, on Tuesday night, iii -consequence of her daughter's marriage. They did not ; get drunk —Kate McAllister and Bose Harrison, the married daughter,deposed to Garry coming home sober; Patrick Cain, forgeman, and Fanny Harrop, the bar- j maid., testified that the antn were sober, and she con- firmed Mr. Swift's statement as to herself.—Gaorge Barnes, an occasional waiter at the Crown and Sceptre Inn deposed to the three men- coming there sober, and I having three pints of beer, on the afternoon of the Mk, and corning sober in the evening with Mrs. McAllister, and ordering a glass of whisky for her, but having nothing themselves. He,. on that occasion, heard a conversation with the police, but could not dis- tinguish the words as there was a partition between him 1 and the constables.—The Chairman : Didn't want too perhaps,—Mr. Smith protested against this remark, observing that if everything on one side were taken As untrue, it would be impossible to conduct cases. He asked for fairness.—The Chairman : You have it—mr. Swift : I must protest against a 'great many remarks here to-day, that I have not been accustomed to hear in court —Thomas Hannan, the man who had married Miss McAllister, and one of the three men at the inn, corroborated the other witnesses for the defence, as to! what took place tiwre.—Mr. Swift said he could cill a ' number of other witnesses, but would now leave the case with the Bench. After about ten minutes'private deliberation, the Chairman announced that they con- sidered that the case was involved in a cernin amount of doubt, and had decided to give the de' nd- ant the benefit of this. The case was dismissed. There I was applause in court, which was immediately sup- pressed.

div.p: "Is it not rather late to ask that question, Elaine r he answered, evasively. "But, do you ?" she aersisted.. . "Yes," he said, huskily; but he would not pain her by adding: "But it Is with a brother's love, rather than a husband's. Will you tell me whyyott ask me, Elaine?" • . • "I have been reading a book of poems," she re- plied, ,"and one of them, affected me deeply. It was of a maiden who wedded a lover whose heart was another's, and she pined away and died. Tell me, Arthur," she cried, vehemently—" did you ever love any other woman T" A spasm of pain crossed his handsome face. He took both her hands in his as he said, slowly: "I will be frank with you, Elaine; it is your due. Now that von have asked me a straightforward question, I will tell you that which I have been sum- ming up courage to tell you for some time past : I have loved before, but I found that the woman to whom I had given all the deep love of my heart was as false as she was fair. I cannot say more about her Elaine, for the very memory of the past is painful. The wound is not quite healed even yet, though I do my best to try to forget. • "I should have told you this on the day I asked youlo become my wife, Elaine," he went on; "but It is 'better late than never.' You do not think the less of me for it, I hope 7" For answer, she burst into tears, murmuring: "But now, and for all time to come, your love is mine, Arthur 7" .

_ "I• shall devote my whole life to you, Elaine," he answered, gravely. "You shall be happy if I can make you so." Even in that moment she noticed, with bitter jealousy. he never spoke of lovit.g her. lie had carefully avoided that. When she reached her own room, she threw her- self down in a velvet arm-chair, with bitter cries. "Another girl's image is in hi. 4 heart—not mine r she sobbed. "Oh, how am I to bear it and live? Seeing her constantly will but fan the name. It must / Oh, if she were but out of the way for ever, his heart would turn to me."

It was a pitiful thought, but she brooded over it night and day, and there was danger in this constant brooding. It was the smouldering flame which wal soon to burst into a raging fire. - ' But from the hour in which Elaine had dis- covered beyond a doubt that lonia Lawrence was Arthur's' first love, lonie has a strange fascination for her.

With the keen eye.; of jealousy, she noted, too, that although lonie Lawrence, was soon to marry Mr. Lyons, there was no love between them. "There is something bark of all this," Elaine concluded: and she resolved that she would find out what it was, at any cost. Another month dragged its slow length by, and at the end of that time a thrilling event happened. (To be continued.)

. MU. 13ESIN1"8 EXPERIENCE OE' BORROWING. Here (writes Mr. Walter Beaant in the "Queen ' ) is a sovereign remedy against the Fiend Borrower. his very simple,and has seldom been known to fail. The borrower comes, and he unfolds his tale; he only wants so much —just so much—tof tide him over. On Monday at ten his difficulties will cease; till then he is in a tight place. Lend him, say, quarter of what he asks; only a quarter; even an eighth, or a sixteenth, will sometimes be sufficient. Accompany the loan with a careful note entered in. a pocket-book recording his promise to repay on a. certain day—generally, as I said, next Monday mot fling at ten. Dcithis very seriously, and inftrm him with much importance that you rely on Nth promise. Of course he will not repay on Monday morning at ten; but he will never come near you again as long as he lives. 7 This rule I have - known to fail twice, and twice only in my own, experience. It was the case of a lady, who. brought a: dismal, woeful story. She wanted .a certain sum .of. money—a twosfigure sum—iinna. -- diately, or she would lose I know not what ; but there wou;d be nothing left to make life desirable. If I would only lend her the money—there was a large sum coming to her that day two mouths—she would give me a bill or 'a promissory note for the amount. She was perfectly certain about being able to repay it on the day named. Very goed, L lent her that sum of money, which of course 1 could not afford to lose. When the day came, the pro- missory note was not taken up. Several years p4ssed by, and then she wrote, asking permission. to inscribe a book to me, as to her very dear old. tiiend. This was too much. Plain truths follows 4 by return post, but I suppose that she is still im- penitent. Another case was that of a young Ameri- can. Ile had the frankest, sunniest, trutniellest face that ever was granted to any young man since the world began. There Was not an atom of guile in that face; he was only about nineteen or tvrenty. Ile wanted, he said, nothing hut one sovereign— - only one sovereign. That would held him on his way to Liverpool. Once there, he had friends who would ship him across to his people in St. Louis. Nis faiber, he said, was a leading lawyer in thst 'city. Once at home he would send back the mot r • immediately. Of course, I ought to huve sent low ' to his own Consul ; but we are arl Weak ;we are all r gullible. It was not much. I lent him.i I e n.oney.. i pointed out to the youth, as one quite old enouga to be hie fattier, and of great experience, that if he Chose to break his word he would not quite break . me, although a writer's is a poor trade, as every- body knows. But,l urged, he would have behind torn, for the rest of his life, the recollection of the fact that lie had been a rogue and a. liar. Up. n which he laughed merrily, begged to shake tne by the band, pocketed the sovereign, and vanisheo. Nor to this day have I hears aught from the lad of he sunny, and frank countenance—that Knight of • • the Cheerful Cheek. So that he has actually got that fact behind him—he can remind liimse;f every nay that he is a rogue.

John, William. and Patrick. Mr. J. D. Buckton cppenred for the prosecution on behalf of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Ctildren. The defendants pleaded not guilty. —lnspector Uphill, agent for the Society, said on the 18th of October, he visited St: Mary's School, which the children attended, and found two of the children there without hoots or stocking a, or covering for their heads. One of them had one old garment on and the other had no shirt. The children were very dirty, as though they had not been washed tor a considerable time. Their hair was full of rennin. Tlie.ehildrn complained that they had no tecakfast, and be took them to their home. He found there no food except & loaf of bread, aad he cut pieces of it for them, which they ate greedily. He found the male defendant upstairs on the bed and ho i id he had teen to work, but there was none for him He inquired from the man's employer and he said he had not been near that morni g. On the 19th of August he fund the three ehildi en at the house . very filthy. There was only one bedroom for the whole family,and there were two mattresves and a few old pieces of rags and sacking for bed lothing. He found the de- fendant the day afterwards drunk in a nei{hbour's house. He could earn 235. a week fhe stuck to work, —Wm. Bamber' one of the School Attembnce officers, grid during five months he had core tently bad the two children, who attended St. Marys brought before him, and found them filthy and ragged. They were not fit to be with she ether children, ano were separated from them. —Jane Daley said the male defendant used to get drunk, tint for the past two months, since the Inspector had warned him about the children, had be,en a teetotaller, and had nought clothes for the children to wear and ' bed. clothing. The defendants spent 14s. to 15s. a week at witness's shop for provisions.—Maggie Will, of Latchford, the female defendant's sister, said she had . been in Its' habit of giving the children food, but it %v.'s when the defendants were cut of work. He had bought clothes for the children, and bed-clothes. She had com- plained about their being neglected.—miss Cole— brook, re:leiter at St. Mart's School, Latchford, said she had • never seen the children respectable except on Walking Day. She bad given them cakes, and got a woman to give them a pair of clogs as they 11(1 nothing on their feet. fhey were at ways ragged, scarcely covered. The smell from them was fsarl lA. She had sent notes to the mother to keep them clean. The mother told her she could not. get F"teicnt food or clothing for them. She had seen vermin on the children. On the 18th of October they looked starved and blue.—The female defendant said she was out at work every day, but she bathed the children evrtl: night and gave neighbours coppers to get them break fast, She could not maintain the children out or her to work herself. husband's money, so had —alderman Sutton Not nut of 235. ?—The luother_rheo-, plied that her husband did not earn that regui.leri y. div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held on Tuesday evening at the Town Hall tor the purpose of wind- ing up the business of the municipal year. The Mayor (Aid. Greenalll presided, and there were also present, Aldermen Francomb, Holmes, Harri- son, Sutton, Wright; Councillors Ashton, Beaman, Blackhurst, Bolton, Donnell, Cannel!, Dixon, It. T. Fairclough, J. Fairclough, Flood, Shaw-Grmen. Greening, Heaton, lienherd, Hill, M.enks, Muir, Flumpton, H. Roberts, Smethurst; Messrs. WhittJe (town clerk), and Longdin (borough surveyor). THE StAXING OF PRIVATE STREETS. Alderman WRIGHT proposed the adoption of the Private Streets Works Act. The matter had been thoroughly discussed, and they were of opinion that it was to the interests of the borough that the Act should be adopted. (Hear. hear.) Councillor HEATON secfuided the resolution. Councillor DIXON asked dis theie had been any diffi- sulty in getting money from property-owners whose streets had been made during the past ten years? Alderman &muss said they had experienced no serious

difficulty. Councillor SIIAW GREIDT pointed out that in clause 17 there was power for any person, who happened to be the owner of any property abutting on to a private street, to mortgage that property for the purpose of providing a proportion of the cost due from him. It struck him that it might be very easy for a person to mortgage the property with the Corporation, and thus •btain easy terms. The TowN CLZRE replied that it had reference only to limited owners of property—tenants for life and child-

Ten. Alderman Winowr, in replying, said as a rule they had not had any difficulty in getting payment. There had, however, been nee or two cases in which they had some difficulty, but he did not wish to mention any name'. They had to incur costs in going to law, and' they did not always win, and they wanted to avoid that for the future. The resolution was then put, and carried unani- mously.

STREET IMPROVEMENT COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the above committee it was resolved that the byelaws with respect to telegraph and ether wires now submitted be approvee and sub- mitted to the Board of Trade for approval. The following report of the Lighting Sub-Committee was approved : —The Lighting Sub-Committee met on the 6th inst. Present : Alderman Wright, Councillors Blackhurst knd Muir. After visiting, the committee re- commended the following alterations and additions to the lamps :—Three lamps in passage behind Bewsey-st., one new bracket lamp in passage at back of Wesleyan tithapel, Bewsey-road. Salisbury-st. ; one new lamp. Passage, Manchester-road, two lamps. Robson-st., re- move lamp opposite No. 5 to corner of passage; one new pillar lamp ; three new lamps in passage behind Robson- at. and Belsby-st. 13Iackhurst-st., remove pillar lamp to north end ; one new pillar lamp opposite No. 2 South- mist side Wilderspool-road, one bracket lamp. Bold-st., tone new 30-candle lamp; remove present lamp from corner of Wilson-Patten-St. Alderman SuproN proposed the adoption of the minutes. _

Councillor BIACKIIURST seconded. Councillor DIXON complained of the awkward position ipf the lamp near the Conservative Club, at the Wino:tar- leigh-st. corner. The MayoE:suggested the advisability of having the names of tne streets affixed to the lamps. Alderman Surrox said he had no doubt that the sug- gestions of Councillor Dixon and the Mayor would be taken into consideration at the next meeting of the com- mittee. .
The minutes were carried. THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.—HOW THE DISEASE

IS SPREAD. A reference to the minutes of this committee appeared in Saturday's " Examiner." The minutes contain a resolution dealing with the accounts, the purchase of corrugated iron and other buildings to be put up at the Hope Hospital ; to the instruction to the Town Clerk to prepare the draft duties of the two committees into which the Ccemcil have resolved that it is desirable the duties and responsibilities of the Sanitary Committee shall be divided ; to the giving of certificates to plumbers for the purposes of the public ealth ' • to the closing of a house in William-street, which had been reported as unfit for human habitation ; to the barricad- ing of Dallam-lane from Owen-street to the bridge of the Cheshire Lines Railway. and to the stoppage of all passenger traffic, and to the instruction of the Town Clerk to prepare by claws to prohibit the blowing of car- casses of animals slaughtered for human food. Aldmman BUTTON moved the adoption of the minute 4 srf the Sanitary Committee. He said that he very much ' regretted that so far there did. not seem to be any abate- ment in the spread of the smallpox epidemic in the borough. Fresh cases were occurring almost every day, but he assured the Council that the committee was doing all it could to stamp out the disease. There was one matter for consolation in connection with the epidemic, and that was the small percentage of deaths. On page six of the minutes there was contained a recommenda- tion that all plumbers be registered, and that certificates be given to such plumbers as in the opinion of the com- mittee were properly qualified to perform plumbing work. Ile thought by that arrangement the public would be assnrel that all work done of this character would be properly executed. (Hear, hear.) Another resolution had also been passed which it was hoped would have some effect in helping to stan:p out the dis- ease, and would keep it within a narrow compass. It was intended to barricade Dallam-lane from Owen-street to a point about the Cheshire Lines Railway bridge. Further barricades would be erected if the committee deemed it advisable. Councillor BEAMAN seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor MUIR criticised the action of the Sanitary Committee with respect to the spread of smallpox. Councillor R. T. BAIRCLOUOII gave it as his opinion that the Committee was not doing everything that was possible to prevent the spread of the disease. Letters' ought to be addressed to every householder asking them to assist in preventing the spread of the disease. The people might do a great deal to prevent the spread of the epidemic if the matter was only prcperly laid before them. He suggested where a case of smallpox occurred that a mark should be made on the house, and no one • allowed to go in until the house was properly disin- ; fected. He would also like a map placed on the wall of one of the meeting rooms of the Council, and the diffe- rens parts where infectious cases broke out marked. ; Councillor llttr. observed that it was a very silly pro- 1 seeding to block up a street. Ho added that he was aware of a case of smallpox in the town at the present mosnent which had not been reported. The MAYOR: It's your duty to report it. Councillor H. Ronanrs thought that it was a matter I of common knowledge in the case of a disease of such a serious nature that the more perfect isolation the more reasonable the likelihood of saving them from the ex- 1 pense of turther outbreaks. Hewes aware that there • ware several gentlemen who bad an idea that smallpox was not contagious. Of course those gentletnen were entitled to their opiniona. If they desired proof of the accuracy of their opinions, they could not do better than voluntarily offer their services in dealing with in. , fected people. The object of stopping traffic was to , make the isolation of the hospital as complete as possible. It was a matter of grave misfortune that they had been compelled to select the present smallpox hospital ; it was a matter for rezrct by all that they had been com- pelled to take a place within the precincts of the borough. It was known that contagion was possible within 1,000 yards of the centre where smallpox was being treated. Councillor HILL I don't believe it. Councillor ROBERTS: "I know what I am talking about." His observations were based on experience gained atlhe last outbreak at Sheffield. Contagion was possible and probable within an area of 1,000 yards of the spot where the disease was being treated. Councillor BTU: It is all tot. Councillor ROBERTS remarked that Councillor Hill might call it 'tall rot," but in spite of all that he (Coun- cillor Roberts) would take care to keep all his connex- ions at least 1,000 yards away from the Hope Hospital, . or anywhere where smallpox existed. It was the duty of every member of the Corporation, and every person who took an interest in the town, to assist the public • officers by reporting every case of smallpox which might come under their natice, to the medical officer of health at once. (Hear, hear.) He hardly thought that there was any case known to any medical man which was not immediately reported. Ile believed the medical men of Warrington were fully alive to the importance of the nature of the disease, and were helping the officials all in their power to stamp it out. He agreed with Coun- cillor Fairclough's suggestions, which he believed would be not only a reminder of the present ostbreak, but would also serve to keep before them the different parts of the borough where infectious disease was prevailing. Such a map would serve to keep before the minds of the Council the presence of the disease far more effectually than any printed report. Councillor Dr. Citemat observed that in the case of a smallpox patient reported last week, the bedding was only removed the previous day. If the disease was to he stamped out, there must be more assistants to get the clothes away. Councillor Boum); informed the Council that he had beard that a smallpox patient had been walking about

the town that morning, with a medical certificate for removal to the hospital in his packet. He was strongly of opinion that when a medical man gave a certificate he ought to see that the case was removed to the hospital. Councillor &taw GREEN recommended that the schools should be disinfected °nee a week at the present crisis. He was in a Sunday school recently. which was used as a day school, and on making inquiries he VCRS informed that the school had not been disinfected for four or five weeks. That was too long a space of time to elapse between tho periods of disinfec- tion. Councillor DIXON remarked that the galvanized build-, ings which had been purchased • by, tne Corporation to provide sleeping accommodation for the nurses at Hope Hospital must either be rotten, or they must have been stolen or bought and never paid for. Such buildings as described could not possibly be purchased at the price demanded, viz., £12.5. (Laughter.) Continuing, he asked to be informed who would examine the plumbers for the puraose of granting certificates of efficiency. Would Alderman Sutton or Councillor Shaw Green for Instance be asked to make the inspectiau ? Dealing with Councillor Robert's remarks that every member of the Council ought to lend his assistance during the smallpox epidemic, Councillor Dixon said (sarcastically) that he would not like to go and help the Sanitary Com- mittee. He would not go unless he had twelve men with him, all of whom were armed with rifles. He knew them. (Laughter.) Councillor BONNIILL informed the Council that he visited Blackburn to see the galvanized buildings. and he immediately saw that the Corporation had a tremendous bargain. In fact, had the Committee not decided to take the property, he would have sent off a telegram the next morning closing the bargain for himself, and he felt convinced that he would have cleared £lOO over the transaction. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BRAMAN said that the Sanitary Committee was very much hampered in its efforts by the morbid curiosity of the public. When Mr. Bloomfield removed a case in some neighbourhoods, he was surrounded by all the neighbours. The house to the vehicle was lined by them, and sometimes he had to wriggle his way be- tween them. On the 19th of October the Sanitary Com- mittee passed a resolution giving the inspector to under- stand that every house wherein occurred a case should be disinfected within 24 hours after the removal of the patient. One of the Councillors had asked why the com- mittee had recommended the barricading of a certain portion of Dallam-lane. In etp'anation Councillor Bea- man said that the only windows in the Hope Hospital that abutted on any public street were those which abutted on Dallam-lane. 'the gates to the entrance of the hospital vc ere in Dallam-lane, and by erecting barri- cades they would cut off communication between the outside public and the inpatients of the hospital. Some very curious things had transpired in the Hope Hospi- tal. He heard of a strange thing the other day. One of the patients had the surprising ingenuity to unravel R woollen stocking and let down the wool. Someone be- low fastened something to it, and the article was drawn up into the hospital. Such a thing he did not suppose that anyone present would countenance. He thought that the Winwiek-st. end of Owen-st. ought to be barri- caded, and also the waste land adjoining Hope Hospital should be effectually barricaded from those persons who were everlastingly loafing about, out of pure curiosity. He thought that those living at the Jockey end of the town would not object to going round Stamford-st. to Dallam-lane. He was confident that the majority or the employes at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' werks would be very pleased at the precaution, and would not con- sider it in the light of a hardship. Alderman HARRISON in face of what had been said in reference to the delay in the disinfection of infected houses, asked to be informed if the resolution that every house should be disinfected within 24 hours had been strictly carried out. Removing the patients was hardly equivalent to disinfecting a house, when the clothes were not removed.

Councillor BEAMAN said that he was afraid the resolu- tion was not carried out, but from what cause he was not in a position to say. Councillor PLITUPTON wanted to be informed who was responsible for the resolution of the Sanitary Committee not being carried out. In the Immediate neighbourhood of the works with which he was connected a case of small-pox occurred. The patient was removed, but no one ever came near to the house from the Corporation to disinfect it fcr a week. What was the use of barri- cading streets when houses were not disinfected and the inmates were allowed to mix with fellow workmen? Councillor FixaTox remarked that one of the chief reasons why the Sanitary Committee deemed it neces- sary to barricade the street was the fact that when patients were removed a whole crowd of people followed the patient, just for all the world as if he were a show. Re did not think that a crowd of reckless people ought to be allowed to approach within 100 yards of small-pox patients. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SurroN said it seemed to him there was a disposition on the part of some 4of the members of the Council to be continually complaining tirst that the Sanitary Committee was not doing its duty and con- tinually neglecting its work. If tkey attempted to do their work by passing certain resolutions they were told that they were doing what was unnecessary. It ap- peared to him that they did not know what the com- mittee should do or what it should not do. Mention had been freely made about the disinfection, but the Coun- cil ought to remember that the resolution was only passed on Wednesday evening. A MEMBEG : It ought to have been passed before.

Alderman SurroN : That gentleman does not do everything on his committee that he ought to e 1.,. Tne committee desired that the disinfectants should be used at the earliest possible opportunity, and he would in- form the Council that they were surprised that this pre- caution had been neglected. They were surprised that disinfectants were not used until some time after the patients had been removed from the infected houses. As soon as this fact was made known to the committee, it was resolved that every house should be disinfected within 24 hours of removal of patients. Since the in- structions were given houses had been disinfected within five hours after the removal. Councillor Bolton had made a remark that a man afflicted with the small-pox had been walking about the• town with a certificate for removal to the hospital. When a Councillor brought such a statement before the Council he thought he should be prepared to produce the name of the medical man who gave such a certificate It re- flected the greatest discredit on the medical officer wile gave such a certificate without notifying the proper authorities. If such a case as the one in question had come under his notice he would have considered that it was his duty to give such information as would prevent anything of a like character occurring again. The sym- pathetic neighbours ought to be informed that they ought not to crowd infected houses. One case had come under his notice where five women, one with a baby in her arms had gone into a room' where a small- pox patient lay. The minutes were then passed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

This Committee reported that the sum of £874 Bs. 4d. was the cost of forming and paving part of Bostock-st., and the Town Clerk was instructed to recover the res- pective apportionments. They recommended that the Chairman and Deputy-Chairman report on the plan sub- mitted by the Ship Canal Company for the construction of a dam across the river opposite the end of River-road, and that they invite the Chairman and Denuty-Chair- man of the Rivers Committee tojoin them in the matter. —The following total apportionments had been fixed : —Passage behind Nos. 2 to 64,Pierpoint-st., £lB5 Bs. 6d., Percy-et., £374 39. 4d. Alderman Wnionr proposed the adoption. He re- marked that he had never known in his experience of the comtntitee more work to be done than had been done during the past year. They were going on most satisfactorily. Councillor HEATON seconded, and the motion was adopted. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTER.

He joined very cordially in everything that had been said regard- ing the manner in which the Mayor had conducted the business of the Corporation. He had shown the utmost liberality in his rulings with regard to members' speeches and he (Mr. Roberts) himself was one of thse who occasionally transgressed the strict rule of debate, and had felt that considerable latitude had been extended to Councillors. The MAYOR thanked the Council for the cordial way in which they had always received him, and the assist- ance they had given him in the discharge of his duties. Re also thanked them for the kind manner in which they had referred to his wife's services. He could not have satisfactorily performed the duties of his office had it not been for the help and suppprt he had received from her. (Hear, hear.) In years gone by she did not care about the place, but since she had mixed with the people of Warrington, she had taken a warm interest in the town in every manner. (Applause.) He had tried to do his best both in the Council and on the bench, where he had always endeavoured to be impartial. He had tried to do his duty, and if he had failed it had not been his fault. div.head: CHESHIRE STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE.
div.p: CHESHIRE STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE.
At a quarterly meeting of this body held at Chester on Saturday, under the presidency of Colonel C. H. France Hayhurst, the quarterly report of the chief constable was submitted.

Mr. R. Howard, a magistrate, observed that out of all the 36 licenses objected to by the police, only six were refused by the magistrates. This was to his mind a very extraordinary thing. He knew the magistates had the interests of sobriety at heart, and professed to want to make the country sober, but the profession and the practice, as shown by those statistics, scarcely corresponded. He would like to suggest, with all due deference to the magistrates, that in deciding these cases, where there were too many public houses and in cases where the police objected, the justices should view the objections with all the seriousness which the cases demanded, and he should like to see in the future the action of the police better backed up by the magisterial authorities.—Mr. James Smith (New Brigh- ton), another magistrate, said he would like to know whether the two out of the six licenses which were ap- pealed against were finally refused. As regards only six out of the 35 being refused, he thought a probable explanation of this would be that objections to renewals were made by the police on the grounds that changes were desirable in the accommodation afforded by these houses.—The Chief Constable (Colonel Hamersley), in reply, said that in those cases where objections bad been made,the justices after careful consideration had found, he supposed, good reasons for granting renewals with the exception of six. He himself was not responsible for the action of the magistrates. As to the two appeals they were both withdrawn. Mr. M. T. Graveson (Liscard) said there had been a diminution of drunkenness since 1885, and the decrease In the quarter just past compared with the correspond- ing quarter of previous years was very remarkable. He believed this was largely owing to the increased exer- tions of the police. He believed that the magistrates were now feeling their responsibility more and more, and were supporting the police better than formerly. This was only the beginning of a good work, and if they continued the measures which had recently been adopted he believed they would soon see a greater decrease in drunkenness. Through the whole of Ches- hire the number of public houses compared with the number of inhabitants was one to every 290, which compared favourably with other counties. He observed that Runcorn had almost one case of drunkenness to every public-house, whereas in every other place in the county they had one for every two public-houses. In nearly all the other places in Cheshire there had been prosecutions against publicans, but in Runcorn there were no prosecutions against the trade. If these figures were transferred to any other form of crime— take, for instance, petty thieving or any other kind of crime—and they discovered that in any district where there was a large amount nf crime there were no prosecutions, he thought there would be no rest until some of the offenders had been dealt with. (Hear,hear.) —Mr. Speakman (Runcorn) said in Runcorn they were in a peculiar position owing to the Manchester Ship Canal. When those works were completed, lie felt sure that drunkenness would go down to its normal position. It spoke well for the publicans of that town that there were no convictions against them. The Chairman said there was no doubt that the jus- tices were trying to see their way clear to get rid of a large number of public-houses as quickly as they could. (Hear, hear.) Colonel Hamersley, replying to Mr. Beckett, said the Deputy-Chief Constable, with his approval, hed sanc- tioned the calling out of the military during the recent disturbances in the salt district. It was resolved that the districts involved in the strike—Runcorn.Northwich, and Eddisbury—should bear the cost of the police ar- rangements.—Preliminary steps were taken with a view to securing better and more ample accommodation at the Chester Assize Courts for witnesses and jurors.

Eleven fires took place in the Borough, the damage being prob- ably about £2,000, mostly covered by insurance. There are 12 cab and hackney carriage owners,and 71 cab and omnibus drivers,7 dealers in gunpowoer,3o dealers in small fireworks, 11 marine stone dealers ; and 24 com- mon lodging-houses in the borougrt, accommodating on an average over 350 per night.

THE LATE LORD TENNYSON.
SERMON BY THE REV. Joas YUNGE..

A Tonnyeon memorial service was held in WycHate Congregational Church on Sunday evening 'when a large congregation assembled to listen to a sermon by the Rev. John Tonge. During the even- ing,, the quartet,. "Crossing the Bar " (Tennyson), was. creditably sung by Mr. and Mrs. Pearson, Miss Ratlibone, and Mr. W. H. Wallington, to music • written Ly Dr. Bridge. This was followed by 'prayer and the hymn written by the late poet, ," Strong Son of God, immortal love," alter which an offertory was taken on behalf of the Centenary Fund of the Cheshunt College, in, which the Rev. John Yonge was trained for the ministry. The rev. gentleman then proceeled with his sermon, the words of the text being "See, the Lord hath called by name Bezaleel,, and Be hath filled him with the spirit of God in wisdom, in understanding, and in knowledge, and He hath put in. his heaq that he may teach." Mr. Yonge said the name of Alfred Tennyson might be substituted for that of Bendeel, as the one whose loss the nation mourned was a teacher, a prophet, as well as an unrivalled poet they might even believe him to have been inspired of God for his great work. The death of Tennyson would cause his poems to be read with considerable interest, and no doubt men would discover in them both new beauty and richer meaning. And that would be indeed well, as a stimulated interest in true poetry was a thing to be greatly desired. There were poems of the Laureate's suited to all sorts and conditions of men. They were all perfectly pure, and there was no taint in them, such as could be only too plainly traced in the writings of some who had been placed high in the ranks of poetic genius. Archdeacon Farrar, in his memorial sermon for Tenny- son, had well said " We thank God that his poetry is absolutely stainless and most no'oly pure." No one could read lennyson intelligently without being elev- ated. Be brought them in closest contact with the beauties and glories of nature : flowers bloomed beaute- ously, and their very fragrance stole upon their sense; streams and rivers glinted and glided down and amid the silent hills, or rolled and rushed onwards and out to , the foaming sea. They heard the distinctive note of every songbird, and well they might, because it ' was said that the poet knew each English ' song-bird's note; they rested in the valleys; they climbed the mountain and inhaled the stimul- ating air; they gazed upon the placid bosom of the lake; they were fanned by the feath- ery zephyr; they bowed to the forceful gale ; they atood awed before the mighty majesty of ocean; and in, through, above it all, they detected the pre- sence and the power of "the one God sad Father Al- mighty. Maker of heaven and earth." He brought them into the fellowship with noble types and ideals of manhood and womanhood, and they seemed to hear the ancient testimony of Genesis enforced and illustrated in his sublime Arthur, " God made man in his own image." "We know not," said Mr. Gladstone in an essay on Tennyson, "where to look in history or in letters for a nobler, and more overpowering conception of man as he might be than in the Arthur of this volume Wherever he appears, it is as the great pillar of the moral order and the resplendent top of human excell- ence." And Tennyson discussed for them the deep pro- blems of humanity, sounding the very depths of doubt, venturing through the gloomiest of its shades, leading them with a brother's hand out at length to the clear unambiguous light, and making them feel from and through all that Paul's great conclusion was invincibly and eternally true, " Now abideth faith, hope, love, these three, and the greatest of these is love." Christi- anity might claim Tennyson without hesitation as one of her finest teachers in this age. Someone had said with perfect accuracy that Tennysan never wrote a hymn, never wrote what could techaically be called a religious poem, but yet he wrote few poems that were not pervaded by a religious spirit, and none that con- travened that spirit. It had been said that his allusionB to war were open to considerable objection from the Christian standpoint, but it should be understood that while Tennyson held in righteous honour the courage and devotion that were the offspring of a true patriotism and could applaud the patriotic soldier as a needful and noble servant of his country, still his references to war, which seemed to revel in it, and to gloat over its ghastly features, were meant to be simply the expression of the character which the poet was depicting, and not the expression of his own cherished idea. Take his poetry all through and its spirit was Christian, its teaching was Christian, its influence was Christian. Tennyson's influence, if not upon theology itself, yet certainly upon the preaching of Christian pulpits, had been very con- siderable, and along with the theolagical teachers of the broader and more progressive tchool, Tennyson had done much in mitigating the severity of cider views and in broadening the faith and hope of Christian people. Tennyson had made plentiful use of the Bible in his poetry. In his poems from end to end no fewer than 300 Scripture quotations had been found. Two books indeed would seem to have been held by the poet in his highest regard —the Bible and Shakespeare. It would have struck many as remarkable that in his latest moments the dying poet should have asked not for the Bible, but for Shakespeare to be placed in his hand. It was not, however, for them to venture any positive or disparaging judgment. That the poet was looking in that hour of nature's extremity for his heavenly Pilot is assured to them in his own words of exquisite pathos that they had had sung to them that night. Those lines were among the latest he produced, written in the advanced evening of his dais, in his 81st year. Clearly they indicated the attidude of his mind. They told them that he was keeping Christ in steadfast view. There could, Mr. Yonge said, be little question that the poem which would ever stand as Tennyson's latest and completest work was that ,which perhaps was least widely read, and least pepularly appreciable. He referred to" In Memoriam." The poem was written as a tribute of supreme affection re the memory of Tennyson's dearest friend. Arthur Henry Hallam was the son of the historian of that name. He was a young man of exceeding and even marvellous promise. He entered upon life at Cambridge the same year with Tennyson, and they became wonderfully intimate, maintaining the most loving and loftily intellectual fellowship. Hallam, during a holiday in 1833, died sud- denly at Vienna, at the age of 23. Tennyson described his death in what was perhaps one of the mcst exquis- itely perfect lines of poetry ever written— God's finger touch'd him, and he slept

The poem was indeed the expression of a grief that had convulsed the whole life of its author. It was impos- sible to quote from that matchless poem so as to convey a just impression of its beauty or its truth. It required to be read and re-read, read at intervals, and with such opportunity for reflection as solitude and leisure afforded in order to receive its spirit and realize the tender force of its teaching. A work that took 17 years to conceive and perfect could hardly be comprehended in a casual and cursory survey. Mr. Yonge added that Tennyson was one more illustration, of which history was full, that the best, wisest, and greatest of men were ever on the side of faith.

Some beautiful verses writtcn by Mr. Corney, head- master of Wycliffe School, were most tastefully sung by Mr. W. 11. Wallington, and shartly afterwards the ser- vice, which had been a very impressive one, was brought to a conclusion.

' On Saturday morning, Mr. George Cooper, nut and bolt manufacturer, Sheffield, who had just drawn £B7 from the London and Yorkshire Bank for wages, called at the Grey Horse Hotel, and put down his cash bag on a bench in the smoking-room. When he 16ft he for- got the bag, but returned before he had got more than 200 yards. The bag, however, had disappeared. Six men went to a Paris wineq.hop in broad daylight, and began billiards. While his companions were noisily knocking the balls about, the need of the gang ran- sacked a bedroom. An alarm tv,.s eased, and the thieves were pursued. Crampon, the leader, pulled out a re- volver, and shot two men deid. The entire gang was captured. Crampon has been sentenced to death, and • the it to terms of penal servitude.

div.head: DRAMATIC SUICIDE OF A STUDENT.
div.p: DRAMATIC SUICIDE OF A STUDENT.

SUDDEN DEATH OF THE AFFLICTED PARENT. A very sad incident is reported from Jassy. The twenty-rear-oil son of Senator Bonachi passed his examination with distinction, last week, and invited a party of fellow-students to celebrate the joyful event. The young men arranged a small concert, and young Bonachi played the violin with much exprea.siou. Before reaching the end of his solo, however, he suddenly threw the bow from him, and, drawing a revolver, fired into his mouth. lie died in a few moments. His father was in Vienna at the time, and fell dead on the spot , when he heard of his son's death.

div.head: SENSATIONAL SUICIDE IN AN HOTEL
div.p: SENSATIONAL SUICIDE IN AN HOTEL

A remarkable suicide has been committed at Charing Cross Hotel, London. A few days ago a lady giving the name of Mrs. Gordon took rooms at the hotel. She ap- peared to have plenty of money, and to be in good spirits. She was visited by a gentleman, with whom she seemed to be on very friendly terms. He seems to have seen her on Thursday night. On Friday at noon, when the chambermaid called the lady, she was found to an unconscious state. She was attired in a tea gown, and had not been to bed. She was removed to Charing Cross Hospital, where she expired on Saturday evening. There is some reason to believe that death was caused by poison. In the room was a letter addressed to the Coroner, expressing her determination to commit suicide. Some extraoriinary evidence may be given at I the inquest.

div.head: INEQUALITIES OF THE LAW.
div.p: THE INEQUALITIES OF THE LAW.

FOUR YEARS FOR TWOPENCE. At the Middlesex County Sessions, on Saturday—be- fore Mr. R. D. M. Littler, Q.C.—George Leaver, 29, carpenter, and William James Halton, 22, labourer, were indicted f*.r stealing from the till of the Nelson public house, Wilton, twopence. Mr. Lawless prose- cuted. and Mr. Purcell defended Halton. Leaver pleaded guilty. The jury found Halton guilty, and Mr. Littler sentenced him to twelve months' imprisonment, he having been several times previously convicted. There were four or five convictions against Leaver, and Mr. Littler sentenced him to four years' pena servitude. Leaver: " You have not heard me. You can't send me 'to penal servitude for attempt, you— vagabond. You ought to have fourteen years yourself." [He was then removed.

div.head: TOUCHING INCIDENT AT BIRMINGHAM.
div.p: TOUCHING INCIDENT AT BIRMINGHAM.

REUNION OF DIVORCED HUSBAND AND WIFE. A marriage will shortly take place in tirmingharn between a lady and gentleman who were man and wife aight Tears ago, but who on the lady's petition' were divorc;ed. Since that time the lady has resided and kept house for her father. She has led a quiet unobtru- sive life since the decree nisi was made absolute, and has steadily refused more than one good offer of mar- riage. Her former and future husband is in a prosper-, our way of business in one of the important cities of the nit North, and there is abundant evidence to show that the fickle waywardness of yo is now lost hi a sober and industrious manhood. That the lady was amply justi- fied in taking, proceedings at the time is shown by the fact that She has miintained an unbroken friendship with her former husband's relatives. Such an example of forgiveness, with an alm,,st sacred devotion to a first love, is but seldom recorded.

BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETE. The annual meeting of Runcorn Board was held on Tuesday night, in Bethesda Lecture Hall. The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood presided. The Rev. div.head: RUNAWAY HORSE AT _RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNAWAY HORSE AT _RUNCORN.

On TbursdaTev,ening, about 7 o'clock, a horse belong- ing tc) the C&operative •Society, took fright in Public Hall Street, and, with the shafts dragging behind, galloped at a furious speed down High Street and across Fountain-square, where it dashed into the window of the Manchester Furnishing Company. Two panes of glass were smashed, and the horse, which is a valuable one sustained considerable injury. Several children had narrow escapes from being knocked down by the animal.

....... PROPOSED LIFE BOAT SATURDAY FOR RUNCORN. Mr. F. NViswall, chairman of Runeorn Board of Com- missioners, has called a meeting for *witty evening,for the purpose of considering the advisabinty of establish. ing a "Life Boat Saturday " in Runcorn, in aid of the Royal National Life Boat Institution. The meeting will be held in the Boardroom of the Town hall at 7 30. Very little advocacy should be needed to obtain t he sup- port of the inhabitants of the port of Runcorn to such a project. WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. A meeting of this Committee was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. H. W. Deacon. The Chair- man announced that Mr. F. H. Gossago had presented 35 volumes, part of the hundred best books mentioned by Sir John Lubbock, which Mr. Gonage had promised to forward as they were published. The Committee cordially thanked Mr. Gossage for his handsome gift. On the motion of Mr. Midwood, seconded by Mr. Robinson, a vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman for his ser- vices during the ,paot year, and the Chairman in reply expressed the hope that the Town Council would appoint the same Committee. Rumour; SONS OF TEMPERANCE

_ On Saturday evening a meeting of the members of the above organisation was held under the presidency of Mr Heeson. There was a good attendance. An excellent paper was submitted by Mr David Smith. entitled,"Who are the most succeessful teetotallers and temperance workers ?" The essayist divided his subject into two parts. He referred to those who abstained because it paid, and really adopted principles of temperance from a sordid motive. He passed severe strictures upon this class. There were, however, those who refrained from taking alcoholic drinks, because they believed it was right to do so. To these all honour, is due, and the la- bours of such men and women had been attended with great success as demonstrated by the army of men who had joined elle ranks of teetotallers .--The reading of the paper was followed by an interesting discussion, . which Messrs. W. Brisbrown. S. W. Timperley, Thomas Cooke, Thomas J. FRAt, and Edward Key joined. Votes of thanks closed an enjoyable meeting.
