div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The triennial election of Widnes Scheel Beard took I place on Saturday last. The‘e were t we've en inliJates for eleven seats, five being Catholics, four Criureti of England, and three Progressive. or unsectarian. There ' was practically no excitement observable,but each party had a considerable number of workers in the ten districts into which the town was divicted for the purposes of the election. There was a polling station at a school in each district, viz., Farnworth, Appleton, Simms Cross.Alhert- roas.l, Warrington-road, Newton,Victoria-road, Waterloo- road, Mersey-road No, 1, and Mersey-road No. 2. The , busiest time was during the afternoon and )ust imme- diately before the poll closed at eight o'clock. The ballot boxes were at that hour conveyed to the Town Hall, where Mr. A. F. Mann, the returning officer; had made arrangements to count the votes on Monday. An extra- ordinary and most unusual difficultyarose to prevent this programme being carried out. It appeared that on Saturday night, Mr., R. Whiteside, the presiding officer of No. 1 polling station in Mersey-road district, which was held at the Gospel Mission Room, was duly sealing up the ballot box with burning sealing wax,when a small portion dropped ,throucli the aperture at the top, and immediately set.the voting papers in a blaze. With all haste the box was broken open and the flames put out, but not before eight papers had been burnt to Ruch an extent as to make them altogether uedecipherable, and therefore they could not be recorded at the counting. In- formation of the unfortunate accident was at once con- veyed to Mr. Mann, who, after due consideration, de- clined to take the responsibility of completing the elec- tion minus these papers, and decided to seek the advice of the Education Dc.partment, in the matter. Accord- ingly, he and Mr. G. H. Danby, the Clerk to the School Board, went to London on Sunday afternoon, and on Monday a telegram was received from Mr.Mann,bidding the officials to prepare for counting on Tuesday. but it was understood that afterwards any of the twelve can- didates could object to the validity of the election. The counting took place on Tuesday morning, and shortly beforetwo o'clock the returning officer declared the result as follows : H WADE DEACON (Church of England) REV. G. A. GARRETT (Church ot England) 3,114 D. LEWIS (Unsectarian) B. BROWN (Unsectarian) REV. J. CLARKE (Catholic) C. E. BARLOIV (Church of England) 2,858 R. SHAW (Unsectrarian) REV. DEAN FINEGAN (C) FLYNN (C) ' S. Quinn (C) 2,278 Dr. O'KEEFFE (C) MAJOR WAREING (Church of England)

Mr. D. Lewis moved a vote of thanks to the return- ing officer, which was spoken to by Father Clarke and Mr. B. Brown, all the gentlemen complimenting Mr.: Mann upon the able and efficient manner in which he liad conducted the election, ano expressing approval of us action in the dithiluity in which he was placed.—ln reply Mr. Mann expressed pleasure that his action had given. satisfaction.
or

" It will be observed that Major Wareing is only defeated by 17 votes, and there is a generally expressed opinion that n 9 the result is so close there ought to be another election in the district, in which the voting papers were burnt, but it is doubtful if this ispractic- able. The total number of votes recorded for a.,e Catholic candidates is 12,131 Church, 11,631, Unsectarian, 8,559, and it is worthy Of remark that with only 500 inn re votes than the Church, the Catholics have secured two more members.which 9)caks volumes for their organisa- tion. With 3,000 fewer votes the Unsectarian party have an equal represeiitation with the Church.

Gossage, in the course of a speech, said when he consented to stand as a candidate, under the auspices of the Liberal Association, he did so thinking it was a right and proper course to pursue, but on considering the matter and Clio possible results, he came to time conclus- ion that an independent policy was the best, as at the present time, in his opinion, politics were allowed to take too great a place in municipal affairs to the detriment of the true welfare of the town. (Hear, hoar.) lie therefore cancelled his agreement with the Liberal Association, with the full intention of entering upon this contest as a free and independent candidate. At the same time it was his ardent wish that their fellow. townsman Mr. Brown should be elected to the Council,, and he therefore determined to withdraw from the con- test and to do all in his power to advocate the cause of Messrs. brown, Smith, and Timmis. (Applause.) Mr. Brown ”'pressed his obligations to Mr. Gossago for his sentiments end his action. Ile (Mr. Brown) did not appear Won- in without being asked, and he held that it Was Lho p liege of Wards to elect their own representatives. (A, plsuse.) It was an honour to be elected by their felloW-townsinen, but for a political caucus to put forth nominees and to take away . the right of the ratepayers to select their own repre- sentatives was doing the town a wrong, and for that reason he stood before them as an independent candid- ate. (Applause.) Mr. Smith said lie was found to have been selected as a candidate by his neighbours, and lie was anxious to go to the Council, if they wished it, as a free man, to do what: he could, according to bits conscience, for %Vest Bank. div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY OCTOBER 29. 1892. "THE MUNICIPAL ELECTI(OB- - . $0 • BATTLER TO BE FOUGHT ID WARRINGTON. A COMPROMISE IS ,AGREED TO. "There ham been a compromise, and no con teats are to take place !" It wassail Tuesday afternoon, and the report ran round the town like ' Everyone knew that it applied to the municipal elections ; and afinost evetyoue, even until that morning, had been anticipating the j.ists anti excite- ments of the November battles , for municipal laurels. An Englishman geueraily Imo in his nature blended, a clear, bold tinge of pugnacity. And hence, amongst us Wa.rrington and Iriali too, by-the-way—there were feelings of hurtful disappointment, and blighted visions, when the report came round. The much-tondled picture of tine. well-printed, mural literature; of brave men willingly inviting itdiiienza and rheumatism in cold 'dark schnolrooms ; and of the candidate, like a volcano pouring out his lava of promises, had vanished like a puff of steam before the wind ! _ There were, naturally, many inquiries as to the cause of the compromise. Moat ot the rank and tile 'ofahe Liberal party wanted to know why had the decision to tight the elections, arrived at by an ag- gregate meeting of the wards on October 13th, been reversed. Some were indignant about it; but when the explanation had been given many considered the step a wise one. During the few days prior to the nominations the leaders of both political parties had beets seriously contemplating the great (hugger of spreading the smallpox epidemic, by .holding public meetings. Indeed, several .•candidates on both sides, had publicly avowed that they would neither bold public meetings nor sanction any canvassing on their account. One candidate—who ' is a retiring Councillor—came to such a decision after a rude experience. He made his way to a friend's house to get his nomination paper filled up. , But on his way he was informed that his friend was suffering, from smallpox, so he turned in the direc- tion of another friend's house. ,But when be saw the epidemic van leaving that friend's house, he turned in the direction of home, fully appreciating the danger which has impelled the two parties to come to a compromise. This compact, it is consider- ed, has been arrived at by a sacrifice on the part of the Liberals, for by the abolition of the contests there vanished a golden opportunity. The terms of the compromise which the Liberals first asked for were that six of the wards—Bewsey, White-' cross, Orford, Latchford, Howley and Fairfield—should not be contested, the Liberals claiming that they were justified in returning their men in the first three wards. As regards the other three wards,Town llall,St. Austin's, and St. John's, it was proposed that they should be con- tested. This proposition was made on the Monday. The Tories rejected it. So candidates for all wards were nominated by both parties, except in Town Hall ward, where Councillor Heaton was re-elected unopposed. All passibility of a compromise seemed now to have fled. Two of the Conservative candidates, Mr. Muir for St. Austin's, and Mr. Shaw for Bewsey, had gone so far as ,to have their addresses printed, and Mr. Muir's had even been posted on the posting stations. On Tues- day forenoon there was a meeting, at the Liberal Club. of Ward Chairmen and Liberal Candidates, at which the ' situation was discussed, the threatened defection of the Irish party having to be consilered as well as the epidemic. At noon, Mr. William Pier- point, Councillor J. H. Fleming, and Mr. John Clay- ton (agent) on behalf of the Liberal patty sought an interview with Alderman Sutton, Alderman Wright, and Mr. John Hainps,in (agent) as representing the Conser- vative party, and expressed their willingness to leave the representation of the wards as before. After consul- tation with the Conservative candidates who had been nominated in the Liberal wards—Bewsey, Whitecross. and Orford—the proposal made by the Liberals was agreed to, with the result that the names of the opposing candidates in all the wards were withdrawn, leaving six Conservatives and three Liberals to be again returned to council. It was agreed that the compromise should in no way affect the elections next year; and that the Liberal party should be allowed to return unopposed two aldermen for the new Council. Next year. seven Liberal and two Conservatives retire from the Council. These are—Town Hall. j. H. Fleming ; Whitecross, H. Roberts ; ilewsey, J. S. Green; Orlord, James walker ; St. John's G.. Blackhurst ;Fairfield, F. Dixon ; Howley, A. Browne ;St. ' Austin's, J. Idepherd (C) ; and Lateldlrd, J. Ashton (C). AT THE TOWN HALL.

street. I cannot have it done, I cannot afford it." (Rear, hear, and applause.) On the motion of Mr. 5, Jackson seconded by Mr. C. Emery,a vote of confidence in the candidates was carded with only one disssrntlen.' A vote of thanks to :the Cilairmin concluded the meeting. THE LIBERAL CANDID kTEi OF SIMM.I CROSS TWA RD. A meetinc in support of MassrA.Milwool, On, and Sadler, was held in the Board School on Thursday night um-lei-the presidenev of Mr. J. 'Taylor. There was a • good attendance and addresses were given Viy each of the candidates named., THE CANDIDATES AND THEIR ADDRESES.

On Tuesday next the burgesses of the borough of Widnes will have the responsible duty to perform of forming their first Municipal Council. And there is no lack of candidates from which to make a selection. There are 32 aspirants for 18 seats, but they are some- what badly divided for, whilst only four candidates are in the field for Farnworth Ward and West Bank Ward, ' there are seven in Simms Cross Ward, six each in Waterloo Ward and Halton Ward, and five in Victoria Ward. The Liberal "caucus " has come in for consider- able blame for introducing politics into the affair, but it must be remembered that the great majority, if not 'he whOle of the town council elections in &gland are fought on political lines, and it is highly probable that had that element not been introduced now, it would have been in the course e a few years, and it is far more honourable to make an honourable declaration at first and have an , open fight. There is certainly some room for coMplaint in the selection made. It would have been a gracious act to have allowed , the members of the old Local Board who were desirous of again serving the ratepayers, to have a seat on the first council, and, at any rate it would have been wise not to have discarded Mr. Brown and Mr. Frank Heyes, who have had a long career of public service. But the inevitable having arrived, it behoves the members of the Liberal party to loyally support their organisation in their initial effort. If it is good that Liberals should make the laws,it must be good that Liberals should administer them. Measures which the , party have worked for and secured are far more likely to be administered in a more generous and far-reaching manner than by that party which opposed their intro- duction. In a spirit of fairness the caucus allotted a certain number of candida.es to the Irish Nationalists, and there is little doubt that their supporters will vote straight. In Ftsrnworth Ward the Conservatives run three can- ' didates who are'Oppesed by Mr. F. tleyes, who comes forward on independent lines. In his address,Mr. Reyes points out that he has resided in the Warcithe whole of his lift and had served them to the best of his ability and on the local Board for many year. If returned he promises to do his ditty in the future as in the past, withour fear, favour, or bias. In Simms Crots Ward the Liberal candidates are all members of the late Board. Mr. Midwood and Mr. Sadler have for many years taken a prominent part in the town's affairs, and havedone yeoman service for the ratepayers. Mr. Owen has not occupied a seat for more than twelve months, hot he has shown a grasp of • , stese various questions brouslit forward during that I brief period, that does him credit, and he would be a I worthy representative of any ward. These gentlemen ! have issued ajoint address, in which they state : • " As representatives of large interests in the town, we are I deeply and earnestly concerned in all matters affecting I its welfare, and are gratified with the thought that the new Council will become possessed of a valuable cor- porate estate, in the Gas and Water undertakings, which ! have been fostered and developed under our care, and they are now about ths Most efficient and profitable in the United Kingdom. The roads, too, have been placed in a very fair state of efficiency, and very many of the streets which were a disgrace to us have been sewered, made and lighted; at a reasonable cost to the property owners, whereby good value has been obtained, and, whilst we are continuing this policy in the 'tamed- diate future, we pledge ourselves—that, if elected, a vigilant eye slial be keut on the spending departments of the Council, and we will esiiecially watch the interests of this important Ward by doing all in our power to further any project which in cur judgment shall advance the comfort and welfare of' the inhabitants." • One of their opponents is Mr. G. After the compromise had been effected by the two parties, on Tuesday, The Mayor formally attended in the Mayor's Parlour, at the Town Hall, at half-past two, when there were also present—Aldermen Sutton and Wright, Councillor Beaman' Mr. J. Wilkinson (one of the representatftres of the Orford Ward), the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), and the Borough Treasurer (Mr. C. Chorley). Alderman &traces, addressing the Mayor, said: Allow me to congratulate you on the fact that there will be no contest in any of the wards, owing to an agreement whieh has been come to this afternoon between the two political parties. There have been withdrawals on each side, and there is, the refore, now no necessity for a con- : we Tway cangratillate ourselves on that fact, especially as a serious epidemic is raging in the town. 1 cativassUig had taken place, and meetings had been held, there would have been gr. ..t danger of the epidemic spreading all over the town. (Ilear, hear.) The MAYOR: I look upon tile present state of the town as very serious, owing to the outbreak Of smallpox and scarlet fever. With one exception, all the s des of work in the town have been discontinued. There WAS a sale of work in connection with the Wes- leyan Cliapel in llold-street, but I believe the promoters were not able to real-ze the amount they wished to do. Personally I had determined not. to attend any political meetings during the present crisis—although as Mayor I should not take any part in them in any case. Had tills cempromise not been arrived at I should have told the Council to-night that, in my opinion, it was very undesirable to hold meetings which might have the ere of still further increasing the epidemic. I am, however, pleased to learn from Aidartnan Sutton that a eoinproinise has been come to, arid [think that it was a right and proper course to take, under the circumstances, by both political parties. I think we have had enough of elections during the present year. Nothing has pleased rise more during my term of office, than to learn that there will ebe no contest. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Ileausts : At the meeting we held this morning I expressed my determination, even if a con- test took place in Ilewsey Ward, neither to canvass my- self not to ask anyone else to do so on my behalf. While getting a nomination paper filled up yesterday after- noon, I called at a house from which a person suffering from small-pox had just been removed to the hospital. A friend who was with me said " This is very unpleasant. We run the tick of taking the infection." After what. [saw then I came to the conclueion that I would neither canvass myself nor allow anyone to cl) so for me. (Hear, hear.) The Matrok : You are perfectly right, and I quite ogres with you. div.head: EMMANUEL CHURCH. SALE OF WORK.
div.p: EMMANUEL CHURCH. SALE OF WORK.

On Wednesday a sale of work in aid of the expenses in connection with Emmanuel Church 'was opened in the church school rooms above Arpley Station. It may be mentioned that since the acce!sion of the Rev. E. S. Reed to the ministry of the church the congregation has largely increased and be has received most encouraging support. Thp school rooms were prettily decorated with Japanese lanterns and umbrsllatsbantere, and other accessories in the why of adornment. In the large room were the principal congregetional stall, pre- sided over by Mesdames Parsons, Page, and Howard and Miss Jessie Booth, the school stall of which Mesdames Annie Gandy and John Allen, Miss Lees, Miss Heald, Miss Booth, and the members of the girls sewing class had charee. Mrs. Reed wife of the Rev. E. 'r. Reed, also had a still lathe same room, this being in charge of herself, Mesdames Richardson and Henry Gandy, Miss Mason and Miss Eva Lees. There was also a refreshment stall in the large room, the ladies who presided at this and in the adjoining tearoom being Mrs. E. Allen, Mrs. Thomas Allen, Mrs. Ashbrook, Mrs. Landon, Miss Landon, Miss Eva Parsons, Miss Hughes, and Miss Harding, assisted by Mr. John Allen, the Sunday school superintendent. Occupying a centre place in the room was the fruit and flower stall, Miss Heron, Miss M. E. Hindley, Miss Hughes (Pad. gate), and Miss Bibby being the ladies who dis- pensed the horticultural products. In the smaller room was a somewhat novel feature, a gentlemen's stall, Messrs. John Allen, T. Allen, E. Allen, W. Parsons W. Atherton, H. and T. Gandy, with the members of the boys' first class having the management of this depart- ment. In the same room there Was a sweet stall, which was under the care of Miss Beatrice Carriage and Miss Sarah Ellison. Among some interesting cutiosities exhibited were a miniature tea service and table, exquisitely manufactured by Mr. F. Randall of ! Golborne-et., the exhibitor, out of "Wesley oak" ob- tained from the City-road Chapel,London, on its restora- tion. He also exhibited other articles made from oa c excavated from the Ship Canal cutting. At the formal opening the proceedings commenced with the singing of the 647th hymn, after which prayer was offered by the Rev. T. Ross—ihe Rev. E. T. Reed then read part of the 12th chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, and afterwards made some remarks founded upon this. By his invitation, Mr. Cicero Smith, of Southport, then in a short address formally opened the sale. Mr. Samuel Page, the ministers' warden, proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Smith, which Was carried by acclamation, and acknowledged by him ; and the dox- ology closed the proeeedlngs. On Thursday the sale was continued, beim opened for that day by the Rev. E. T. Reed. The proceedings were commenced with the singing of the 176th hymn, Miss Evelyn Hughes accompanying on the piano, after which , the Rev. Mr. Reed prayed; and then he read part of the 35th chapter of Exodus, recordincr the free gifts of the Israelites to the tabernacle. Mr. Reed said the portion of Scripture he had read bore is certain relation to the kind, of work in which they were engaze.l there, and though they 'did not live under the Mosaic disuens di in, it was interesting to find that in the days of whi:th lie had read there were efforts of a similar character made for the benefit of the House of God. Though the gifts brought together by the Children of Israel for the House of God were not to be sold for the personal use of those who purchased them, yet the principle was much the same, and God's work was done practically in the same way that day. They would all be glad to know that the results of the previous day's sale had exceeded the most sanguine anticipations. in addition to the money they had raised, they had had donations kindly sent, £2 by Miss Kendall, of Cheadle, £1 is, from Mr. R. Pier- point, 51. P., and a large parcel of materials from Mr. Walter Gibb, of Eccles, which would keep the ladies sewing class employed for the next 12 months at least. £2O worth of goods had been sent for Mrs. Reed's stall from places outside Warrington. They had come from as far north as Edinburgh, as far south as London, as far east as Sheffield, and as far west as Southport. Thanks were due to the ladies and all others who had helped with such earnestness and zeal to make that sale such a success salt had been. After an experience of Christian work in various parts of the country, he did not know that lie ever saw anything carried through , with greater zeal or enthusiasm than that sale of work had been. Generally speaking,with regard to the church and schools they were very greatly encouraged in their work, and lie wanted to say with all thankfulness to God, that during the present year He had blessed them in a most wonderful way. The special feature which had been of such great encouragement during the past year had been the work amongst the young. He declared the sale open for the afternoon. The Doxology cncluded the proceedings. On Thuesday evening Mr. Page, on behalf of the stall- 114Iiirs and friends, presented to Mr. Reed, one of Mr. gas stoves, a beautifully finished article, al.s.iring Mr. Reed that it was an expression of the I esteem and lis rtfelt affection of those who had subscribed for it. Mr. ltsed, who was completely taken by sur- prise by this manifestation ot kindness, expressed his thanks for this pleasing mark of consideration. The sale was continued on Fritav eveni,ng, being re-opened liv Mr. Reed, and the results at the close far exceeded time most sanguine anticipations of the pro- moters.

div.head: REVOLVEIt NUISANCE.
div.p: THE REVOLVEIt NUISANCE.

, • A WOMANiSHOT AT RUNCORN. jlefore \Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, Robert Stevenson (16), Pennington's Row; Henry Rhead (10). and Earnest Rhead (17). brothers, of Thomas - street, were Charged on remand with having on Sunday, the 23rd inst., unlawfully and wantonly fired off a gun or pistol within fifty feet of the centre of a cer- tain pubic carriage was or cartwas. , to the injury or personal danger cf the persons then travelling thereon. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys defended. When previously , before the Court on Monday, the prisoners were charged with the more seriousbffence of inflicting grievous bodily harm upon Mary Alice Corker, wife of a shoemaker liv- ing in Union-street, but this charge had been reduced. It appeared that on Sunday afternoon anout half-past two, Mr. and Mrs. Corker were walking along the fields in the direction of Rock Savage, an.t when near the smithy known as the " Black flat " they heard several shots fired behind them. Mrs. Ce ker cried 'tut "Oh Fred, lam shot in the side." Mr. Cm.ker turned round a ncl saw the prisoners about, 80 yards a was, and saw one of them fire a revolver iiCINIA the railwny. He found that a bullet liad penetrated his wife's jacket and had glanced off her corsets, which had probably saved her life. Henry' Rhead came up to him and denied having been engaged in the shooting, and he afterwards assisted Mrs. Corker to Runcorn, Wliil her husband went in pur- suit of the other prisoners. He failed to capture them. Information was given to Inspector Cooper, who appre- hended the prisoners, and tound a ball cartridge in Stev- enson's trou.ers pocket,and at his lodgings he found it box emitaining 42 similar cartridges. Stevenson said he had thrown the revolver into a quarry at Runcorn Heath, but a long and close search by Inspector Cooper failed to bring it to light. Mrs. Corker was seriously affected by the shock, and for some time she was in a critical condi- tion. On Thursday Stevenson pleaded guilty and the other prisoners nJt guilty, hut as the prosecution failed to prove that the revolver was fired within the fifty yards specified, the prisoners were discharged, Stevenson being allowed to withdraw his plea.
The cost of the distribution of the Friends' Russian Famine Fund has been £.579. This is wholly defrayed by the society itself out of its ordinary funds.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.

Now that a number of new Liberals are being appointed on the IVarrington borough bench, it is to be hoped that the rule which has hitherto pre- vailed—the more magistrates the worse attendance —will not continue to obtain. The spectacle of the court being kept waiting for lialf-an-liour tor want of magistrates would be a still greater scandal in the future than it is now. But I believe the new Liberal magistrates will not stultify the town by minimising the advantages of their appointment through absence from their duties. I believe they will be working and not mere ornamental members.

In this connection I may mention that, on Wed— nesday morning, there was another exemplification of the remissness of the borough magistrates in point of attendance. At ten o'clock the hour for commencing business, only Mr. John Fairclough was on the bench ; and the court wiv, delayed 20, minutes till another magistrate—in the person of Mr. Geddes—was hunted up. The fault is not so much unpunctuality as not coining at all until a police officer on one of the frequent scouring expedi— tions, which police officers hare to undertake to bring magistrates to court, informs them that the presence at court of. an additional justice is im— peratively required.

There has been a great deal of remark in the town about fear and panic being the use of a large part of the disease that is prevailing. Tnere is no doubt whatever that great apprehenaion of catching an ailment is conducive to infection, hut to judge from what was stated by l,ouncillor Beaman and Alderman Sutton at the Council meet- ing on Tuesday, one might almost suppose that so far from panic about smallpox being general, there are a very large number of people in our midst, who are sodefiant of all danger from the prevailing epidemics as almost to court disease and death. It is difficult to put any other construction on the conduct of the hundreds of people who hang about the Hope Hospirahand follow the patients conveyed thither, as though there were some weird atzrae- non in the loathsome malady of smallpox, and all its attendant, unpleasant incidents. Barricades have and are to be erected by the Corporation, to rrevent people from crowding about the ho:pital, but even this, I understand, has not been a com- plete preventative, for some adventurers have absolutely had the hardihool. to climb them in order to c,onimunicate with the patients.

Weak-minded, hysterical fear of infection is bad enough. but marked curio:4r.), Po strong as to over- ride that common instinct of self-preservation which is the first. law of nature, is abont as deplor- able a form of mental disease as the other. Who can tell what mischief may have been wrought by these reckless adventurers who hang about the small-pox hospital and small-pox patients, and may convey a disease to hundreds while escaping contagion themselves. One would think a small-pox patient would be shunned like a leper, except where neces- sity prevented it. But, there is no accounting for human perversities and contrarieties, My impres- sion is, that there is an immensely great deal more incipient insanity in the world than is commonly supposed. I was reading the other day, that even birds will flee from the neighbourhood of a pesti- lence. But there are numerous human beings who will rush into its very midst.

I see that Mr. 3latkin,so well-known among trades unionists of this town from his appearance at their meetings, has been appointed a member of the Liverpool borough bench. This encourages me to hope that the application of the Warrington Trades Council for the appointment of working-men on our own local magistracy may be further enter- tained.

The memorial service to the late Laureate at Wycliffe Church, on Sunday, was in every way worthy of the occasion. There was a crowded con. gregation ; and the Rev. John Yonge preached a sermon which was as powerful as it was interesting It showed that he had studied Tennyson to some purpose ; and that he fully appreciatPd the beauty alike of his life awl his works. Mr. Yonge spoke of the quotation— God's finger touched him, and he slept— as being "one of the most exquisitely perfect lines of poetry ever written." It certainly is very fine; but it suggests, by its structure, a more famous line by an earlier poet. I refer to Richard Crashaw,who died in Idso, and who, in a single line, thus des- cribes the miracle of turning water into wine—
The conscious water saw its God and blushed.

I understand that the modest " AC, "attached to the toot of one of the memorial hymns, stands for Alfred Corney, tile esteemed head master of Wycliffe Schools. He has no need to hide his light under a bushel, for his hymn is a long, long way above the average. Mr. Corney must let himself be heard again. Here are two of the verses : Star-gleams across the sky ! The fresh'ning breeze awakes ! Day dawns, and all life's shadows fly, The morning breaks! Oh sunrise fair ! Oh morning star ! Oh light of life beyond the bar ! Safe home, safe home in Port ! The heavenly haven won! Through cloud and darkness safely brought, Life's voyage done ! Oh vision fair ! Oh wondrous grace! My Pilot mPets me face to face.
Still harping on Tennyson, I have been struck with the way in which a leading Scotch journal has been taken to task for quoting—
Theirs not to -make ieply, Theirs not to reason why—
as foil OWS :-

Not theirs to make reply, Not th.iits to reason why, ke. Still, worse things have happened at sea, and even in connection with eulogies of the late poet. I observed how one editor, in a leading article spoke of Tennyson's death being a reslibation of his own beautiful lines which run Now more than ever seems it rich to die, To cease upon the midnight with no pain. Beautiful the lines certainly are, but they were not penned by Tennyson ; they were written by Keats. MERLIN.

div.head: OLDHAM HOltitOlt.
div.p: THE OLDHAM HOltitOlt.
INQUEST.

At Oldham, on Monday, the inquest was resumed on Mary Jane Mellor, whose body was found under the stairs at her house in Hollis-road. Deceased's husband, who is in custody on a charge of murder, was present, and cross-examined the witnesses very coolly. Emma Chadwick, who lives near the prisoner, said the latter asked her recently what people wrre saying about his wife. She replied they said that either he had murdered her or she had gone away with another fellow. He said she should take no notice of them. Lizzie Sunderland said she had been keeping company with prisoner about eiohteen months. On August 30th she went to Overden rear liallifax, and prisoner visited her on September 3r.1, remaining all night. She indignantly denied that oil thi4 and other occasions she covered him up on the sofa before she went to bed. Prisoner said he had slept at this witness's house every night since the 4th Septem- ber, except five nights. Sarah Sunderland, mother of the last witness, said prisoner stayed at her house on the night preceding the discovery. Constable Ambrook stated that when he arrested the prisoner he said, " suppose you know what I have come for ?" lie replied. " Yes, it's all right." The jury returned a verdict of wilful murder.

div.head: HIGHWAY OUTRAGE.
div.p: A HIGHWAY OUTRAGE.

AN OLD WOMAN SHOT AT AND MALTREATED. middle-aged woman, named Duffet, was returning to Plymouth on Friday night with groceries when she was fired at on the highway by a man because she would not give him her money. She fell from the shock, and the man, after striking her with a heavy stick, stole 16s. from her pocket and decamped, leaving her in a serious condition. It was supposed that the man was an artil- leryman, but though the soldiers of three forts in the vicinity have been examined, no clue has been obtained.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE. COURT..

SATIIRDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (chairman), Alder- man Chandley, Mr. H. Garnett, and Mr. John Geddes. ABSENT FROM TRAINING.—Richard Neild was charged with being an absentee from the annual training of the 3rd Cheshire Militia during 1891 and 1992.—C010ur- Sergeant Rayner, of the 3rd Cheshire Militia, recognized the prisoner as having been absent from the annual training of the regiment from 1891.—Prisoner said he had been to sea, and when he returned the militia had broken down."—The officer stated that a month prior to the training a notice was sent out to every militia- man calling his attention to the date when the regimext assembled.—Prisoner was fined 40s. and costs, or in default, a month's imprisonment with hard labour. THEFT OF PAPERS FROM THE CENTRAL STATION.—John Baguley, a boy, 14 years of age, as charged with steal- ing a parcel of papers from the Central Station, some time between five and six o'clock on Tuesday afternoon. —The prisoner pleaded guilty.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan stated that the papers produced were put on the platform of the Central Station about four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon for a newsagent named Thomas Locker, of Latchford, and a woman named Mrs. Kay, who resided in Fennell-tit. When the papers were sent for they were missing, and the matter was reported to the police. Inquiries revealed the fact that the prisoner had sold a parcel of papers to a young woman named Booth, representing that they were old papers. Witness found the prisoner and charged him with the theft. In reply he said "I only took two lots; one on Monday night, and one on Tuesday night. I sold one for 3d. and the other for Bd."—lt was stated that the people who bought the papers were very respectable, and when they found they were new ones, they 'nought them to the police station.—Miss Booth stated,in reply to the Bench, that she did not examine the papers before she bought them. The papers were bought for charity's sake.—The local agent for the " Liverpool Courier " stated that the prisoner had had papers from him which he had never paid for. Their agents had complained about parcels going astray from the station for seine time past. He had noticed the defendant on the stations on many occasions.—The Chairman said the prisoner would be detained in custody until Sunday morning. They had tried to save him from going to gaol, or a reformatory, but if he came before them again he would not escape so easily. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) Alder. men Sutton, Harrison and Wright, Francomb, and Mr. F. Monks. Dug.—John Morris in Bridge-st.,on Saturday night. --Dismissed. Hallam AND DISORDSRLY.-Elin, Bentley, in Sankey- at., that night ss. and costs—George White on Friar's Gate, ss. and costs.—John Conway, in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—Ellen Delrioze in Winwick-st., on October 15th, IN.—George O'Brien, in Priestley-st., on the 18th init., who would have assaulted the constable, as he said, but for three young men, ss. and costs. Ann Davies, in Percival's Fold, on the 19th inst., ss. INSANITARY PREMISES.—Mary Lyons and John Fiddler, both of Filling's Court, was charged by Mr. It. Norman, nuisance inspector, with having an outbuilding in an .objectionable condition. The cases were adjourned for a fortnight.—Hannah Map, 3, Stanley-st., and Michael Lyons, 7, Stant ey-st., were charged with like o ffences and fined ss. each.
TvEsnes.—Bef ore Mr, R,Garnett (chairman) and Mr.
E. J. Guest.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Cases of irregular at- tendance at school were dealt with as follows :—John Fiddler, labourer, Dial-it.. fined 2s. 6d. ; Michael M'Kenna, labourer, Lord Nelson-st., 55. ; John Jones, joiner, Gladstone-st., ss. ; James Moseley, wiredrawer, Lovely-lane, ss. ; Martin Dolan, labourer, Gee-st., 2s. 6d.; Ann Mellor, laundress, Foundry-st., 2s. 6d. SENT TO AN INDUSTRIAL ScHooL. —Patrick Ward, son of James Ward, labourer, Ship-yard, who, it was stated, had got beyond his parents control, was sent to Father Nugent's school, Liverpool. TICE POLICE COURT MISSIONARY OFFERS HIS SERVICES. —John Mcdonald was summoned in respect of the ir- regular attendance of his son William. Mr. Taylor, the Police Court Missionary, offered to take the boy to school for a fortnight, and the CASA was adjourned to see whether any improvement was made in his attend- ance. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. John Fairclough (chair: . _

man), and J. Geddes. Malts AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Walsh, from near Oldham, drunk and disorderly in Fennell-street, the pre- vious afternoon, was fined ss. and costs.—Andrew Duffy in Buttermarket-st., that morning, 53. and costs. BREACH OF THE EDUCATION ACT. —rile adjourned case of Martin Carey charged under a warrant with not send- ing his son regularly to school, and whose wife on the previous occasion said the lad was in Ireland was called. Mr. Riley, the school attendance officer now said the lad had been in Warrington, and had never been in Ireland. —The defendant was fined ss. Tau IZSDAY.—Before Al lerman Chandley (chairman) and Captain Ridgway. DRONE AND DISORDERLY. —George Hopkins, in Arnolds yard, off Haydock-st., the previous day, 33. and costs. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White (Chairman), and Alderman Harrison. DEFICIENT SCALES.—Richard Blezzard, 15 Grammar- street, off Canal-street, Ancoat, was charged with having defective scales on his stall in the Market at Warrington. Inspector Place proved the case. Be told Blezzard the scales were defective six weeks previous to the date as to which he charged him.—The defendant said on being in- formed that the scales were unjust he went to Manches- ter, and got a loop put on one side ot them. Mr. Place in answer to Alderman Harrison said the alteration would not correct the fault of the scales.—The defendant was fined £1 including costs, and had to forfeit the scales. _ _ .

CHARGES OF CRUELTY TO HORSES.—Wm. El. Leach, farmer, of Lower Whitley, was charged by Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., with allowing a horse to be worked whiiL! in an unfit state on the 12th inst. Mr. P. Davies (Messrs. Davies and Forshaw) appeared for the defence. Mr. Dowty said the horse was drawing a heavy cart loadod with potatoes, and was very lame in the near fore leg, and suffering from a dropped sole, which was nearly on the ground. The foot was very hot and inflamed, and steam was rising from the inflammation. P.C. Dean COTToborated.—Mr. Davies contended that a dropped sole, was not lameness.—Alderman Harrison said it was generally regarded as such.—Mr. Davies said it was like a corn, and a man might suffer nothing from a corn. The horse had got stiff with standing two hours in the market. He invited the Bench to examine the horse. —Daniel Massey Wilkinson, farmer, High Whitley, said he had known the horse close on 5 years. His farm ad- joined the defendant's, and he constantly saw the horse. It had never had any lameness or inflammation. It would go stiff with standing two hours in the market.— The defendant said the horse had had shoes made which were expressly adapted for dropped feet.—Mr. Wilkinson stated that he saw the horse on the day in question, and observed no lameness.—Thomas Dutton, grocer, Whitley, said he had known the animal three or four years, and seen it very frequently, and never knew it to suffer from anything detrimental ot be ill-treated. He also deposed that on the date in question he saw the horse in Warrington market and it was only stiff. Mr. Leach WU a man of humane character.—The Bench gave the de- fendant the benefit of the doubt and dismissed the case.— John Murphy, 20, Gossage-street, Widnes, was charged

with cruelty to a horse, by working it in an unfit state, on the 12th inst., and fined ss. and costs.—John Bell, of Orford-street, was similarly oharged as to the 17th inst., and James Cottam' 9 Howley House was charged with allowing the animal to be so treated.—Cottam was fined 20s. and costs, and Belittle costs. _ _

AssauLTs.—:John Lawrenson, 1, Providence Place, was charged with assaulting Jane Tickle, 5, Providence Place, on Saturday. The complainant said she went to the house where the defendant lodged, to obtain some clothes from her, when he kn.cked her down, and knocked a tooth out, and kicked her on the thigh.—The defendant said she drew a knife to him. She came in drunk, and begaß cursing the landlady, and hit her and pulled her into the scullery. She was bleeding in the face; and shouted to him to take her off. and he did so, and in doing this pulled some hair off her head. Then she drew a knife, and slightly cut him on the arm. She collared him by the shirt and pulled it over his head, and he struck her.—Mrs.Crosby,the land- lady, said the defendant came drunk and with ad oath demanded hcr money. She was in the habit of leading money at so much in the shilling. She was drunk. Witness corroborated the complainant generally.—Tickle was summoned on the charge of assaulting Mrs. Crosby, and denied touching the complainant.—Both cases were dismissed, the defendants having to pay 2s. costs each.—Bridget Dowse, 6, Angel Yard, was charged with assaulting Mary Clarke on Saturday last, and Clarke with assaulting Dowse. Clarke said Dowse pulled her off her own door by the hair of the head and knocked her senseless to the ground.—Dowse said she had married an Englishman, and the people in the neighbourhood persecuted her on this account, saying they would have no Englishmen there. Clarke pulled the hair off her head.—The defendants were each bound over to keep the peace, and each had to pay her own costs.

ANornart Wommes Row.—Jane Adams, wife of John Adams, 12, Sharp-st., was charged with threatening Martha Tickle, 11, Sharp-st. In the evidence on both sides the use of most horrible and scandalous language was alleged against both parties ; and women's tongues were vigorously clamouring against each other in Court during the case.—The defendant was bound over to keep the peace. CHARGE OF WIFE DESERTION.—James Appleton, now of Manchester, was charged by Elizabeth Appleton, of Baxter-st., with deserting her. The case had been ad- journed to allow the defendant an opportunity of obtain- ing a medical certificate that he was unable to work ; and he now produced this. They charged each other with misconduct, and both denied it.-118 was ordered to pay ss. per week.

div.head: DARESBURY PEI FY SESSIONS. TIJESDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Long (chairman) and H. Neild.
div.p: DARESBURY PEI FY SESSIONS. TIJESDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Long (chairman) and H. Neild.
DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Joseph Dutton, drunk and disorderly, at Grappenhall, on October 24th, was fined 2s. 6d.

DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES .—Michael Ryder, of Grappenhall, and Patrick Gallagher' of High Lagh, were charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of John Hewitt, the Ram's Head, Grappenhall, on the 24th inst.—P.C. Millington deposed to finding the two defen- dants drunk on the premises, Ryder lying on his back in the yard. He brought him out to take him home, and when they got to the canal, Ryder said he would make him swim, and got hold of him by the legs,and struggled with him. A man named Ditchfield came up and witness left him, then Ditchfield left him and he slept where he was till the evening. Callagher made a statement that he and Ryder had been drinking together for two days. On the day in question Ryder and he went to the Ram's Head, the former being sober when he went in, but staying till he was drunk. They had about 15 quarts round, commencing at seven o'clock in the as 'lining, and in the afternoon Ryder was drunk avid the boatman and he got fighting, and the boatman knocked him down. Witness brought him out and laid him among a lot of shavings there, and witness gave him a bottle of soda water to sober him. (Laugh- ter.) The officer came and "copped "him lying on the floor.—P.C. Millington, recalled, confirmed the state- ment that Ryder and the boatmen had been fighting.— Ryder was fined ss. and costs and Callagher ss. DRIVING Wintour REINS.—Wm, Shaw, for driving a cart without reins at Dutton, on the sth inst., was fined 2s. 6d. AN UNLICENSED TRACTION ENGlNR.—WilliamShaw was charged with usiNg a traction engine at Walton, on the 10th inst., without having a license for the same.— P.C. 48 proved the case, and said the defendant stated that he had a license for Lancashire but none for Che- shire.—lt was pointed out that a license was necessary for each county that the engine was used in.—The de- fendant was fined 40s. and costs.

P•ACHINCL—Peter Berry, of Latchford, was charged that he, •n being searched by P.C. Millington, on the 19th inst., on his coming from game land at Grappen- hall, a rabbit was found upon him, supposed to have been taken on such land.—Millington deposed to meet- ing Berry coming front the land early on the morning of the 19th inst., and finding in his pockets a warm rabbit and newly cut pegs. The defendant an hour previous had gone in the direction of the land with a gun in his pocket. He did nothing but poach, and was well-known in Warrington as a poacher.—The defendant was fined 10s. and costs.

BREACH OF THE EDUCATION ACT.—Richard Wilkinson, of Budworth, labourer at the Northvrich Chemical Works, was summ.ned for neglecting to send his two children regularly to school.—A. fine of Ss. was imposed.

Of the Lancashire cup competition, the " Athletic News" says : The difficulties which beset the path cf the Lancaster County Committee in their endeav- ours to classify the clubs entered for next season's contest have beceme modifie Ito a certain extent by the step taken by two of the organisations. The withdrawal of St. Helens " Recs." and Manchester Rangers made room for the more ambitious juniors, and with the pro- motion which became necessary, the hopes and aspira- tions of some club officials were advanced a stage nearer realisation.

The reason the Manchester Rangers withdrew from the competition was not because they were dissatisfied with the Committee's classification, but simply from the fact that they are not so wealthy as some other clubs, and consequently they could not fane the expense which repeated journeys to the north of Lancashire would entail. They were wise enough te withdraw before bankruptcy overtook them, but they would have shown more wisdom and greater discernment if they had never entered.

Quite a different cause impelled the St. Helens Recreation to withdraw, and every footballer who is at all I cospnisant of toe standing of the " Recs." in football circles is ready to admit that they have been badly treated. The fact alone that they are occupying a place in this season's contest should have been sufficient to ensure their inclusion—it has apparently served some clubs in good stead—but as regards merit they stand so much higher than others who have been selected, that the whole thing looks like a piece of favouritism which we never thought the Lancashire Committee were capable of.

Just to prove how the Recreation have performed against seven of the First Division clubs during the past four seasons we append a tabular statement, which shows at a glance the consistant form they have exhibited during that period, and the position which they are entitled to : For Agat. WOL GT G T Broughton Rangers 4 0 0 5 9 1 1 Barrow 6 0 0 10 10 2 2 Oldham Swinton 1 0 3 2 0 4 4 Tyldesley Wigan 2 3 2 4 6 1 2 Warrington

Apart from the best Lancashire clubs, St. Helens "Recs." have also met organisations of the highest class of Yorkshire, and in the four seasons have won just one hundred matches against forty-three lost, and nineteen draws.

The sensation of Saturday's League games may be set down 83 that supplied on the banks of the Wear. The champions have been upbraided by their friends for their indifferent display against Accrington a week ago. Smarting from the shafts of ridicule and taunts of idle- ness, they buckled on their armour on Saturday, and made complete hacks of the hardy sons from Stoney- lane. West Bromwich Albion appeared at Sunderland with a record of only one defeat, hut this was made into two, the severity of the defeat making it all the harder to bear.

Sunderland are veritable gluttons when they set themselves seriously to work. For verification refer to Accrington, Everton, Aston Villa, and West Bromwich Albion. Those who have noted the sturdy defence of the " Throstles" this season must have been amazed to learn that the League champions had scored no fewer than eight goals against the English Cup holders. Only once last season were the Albion colours captured eight times in one afternoon, and that was in an exhibition game at Perry Barr. Sunderland will have a wondei- ful goal record at the end of the season at the rate they are going.

They get magificent gates at Goodison-road, Liver- pool-14,000 there on Satuiday—but it is rarely indeed that the spectators have the satisfaction of witnessing a victory. How different this to a couple of seasons ago. Accrington always give Everton a hard game, and last week end the "reds "rose to the occasion in their, old sweetS ay.'''. They improved on their defeat pf last March by drawing with the "Liverpool idols," which may be set down as one of their best performances Since the present season came in. The team are going well, considering their indifferent start.

• The retrogression of the Blackburn Rovers received further confirmation. From being certain goal-getters, as in past seasons, they have degenerated so much that goals are now a scarce commodity. Jack Southworth was again an absentee, and they were beaten pointless. Derby County had not only a decided pull from a scor- ing point cf view, but beat them in play generally. Well may the followers of the old club cry out for new blood. The Rover were never so low down as they are now, and the outlook is dreary in the extreme. Let us hope for brighter days.

Whilst their dearly beloved neighbours'were demolish- ing one Cheshire team the St. Helens town club were entertaining another one, Stockport. The " hatters " had their strongest team up, but they were simply not in it with Cross's fine combination. The "Saints "have the strongest team that ever represented the club, and they believe they could make a very creditable show against the first division clubs in the Cup competition. Cross himself, was in magnificent form, and besides running in a try from his own half, had a hand in each of the other four tries scored.

Points do not seem to be easily obtained in the Lanca- shire Cup competition, but St. Helens " Recs." are ex- pecting to knock a couple out of Oldham to-day. The " Recs." went to Dukinfield last week end, and piled up a score of three goals and four tries to nothing. Their old half-back, Pilkington, was given another trial, and cams off splendidly,scoring himself,and giving May, the new centre, opportunities, which he utilised to the tune of three tries.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. OCTOBER 29, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. OCTOBER 29, 1892.

unsatisfactory, whilst the backs, with one exception, were not showing the hest of form, and, consequently, Tyldesloy were constantly making dangerous inroads into Warrington territory. From one of these rushes Miller picked up, and running strongly got a splendid try. Bate, on behalf of Warrington, was showing up very prominently, and after several effective pieces of work, dodged beautifully into Tyldesley quarters. The visitors had somewhat the Wet of it afterwards, but Bate generally came to the rescue, Warrington winning ! by 1-1-2 to 0-1-1. WARRINGTON RANGERS V. WIDNES RANGHRS.—PIayed on the Lovely-lane enclosure on Saturday last. The , home team lest the boss, and Savage started the oval. From the first scrimmage, Widnes attacked, hut fine play by Hamblett 'and Price averted and serious danger. Eventually Warrington pressed, and strong forward play forced the Widnesites to concede a minor. After the interval both sides played with great dash, the hoinesters having by far the best of the game, bot failed to score, and the game ended in a draw, Warrington one minor, Widnes nil.

WARRINGTON PARISII CHI/ItCH v. MOS& BANZ (MMUS). —This match was played at Warrington on Saturday. The weather was anything but agreeable,, for about the time fixed for commencing, rain and hail fell heavily, rendering the ground very heavy going. Play during the first half was of a very even character, neither side being able to obtain the lead, and on the restart it seemed likely that no scoring would be done, for the. game still continued of a give-and-take nature. Toward's the close however; the homeaters roused themselves,. and Carey scored after a grand run, and the cheers which greeted him were renewed when he placed a goal. The Widnes- ians tried hard from this point to get on equal terms, but to no purpose, and at the end of a tightly contested game the score was :-'—Parish Church, one goal ; Moss Bank, nil.

SL Main's T. STOCKTON Ef SATE LHAOI3II MATCH. Played at Arplev. The visitors kicked off, the ball being well returned, the game settled down in the visi- tors' half. The Saints' forwards, playing up strongly, kept the ball near the visitors' line, Cross relieving slightly, but the Saints' rushed the ball back, and Bed- dall scored, Efelsby kicking a grand goal. Soon after Thomas got over, but the try was disallowed. Half time was called, the Saints leading by five points. On changing ends the visit)rs had the best of the play, the Saints defending well. Roughley and Hassell getting in some nice kicks, the home forwards rushed the ball into their opponents' 25. Broady, for the visitors, put in a strong run into the Saints' half, where, after some scrimmaging, the ball got loose, Rathbone scoring, Cross failing at goal. The Saints won by five points to two.

RUGBY. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE COMPETITION. WARRINGTON v. TYLDESLEY.

Since the inclusion of Tyldesley in the above competi- tion, which took place last week, the meeting between Warrington and Tyldesley has had additional interest lent to it. The teams met on tke Tyldesley enclosure on Saturday in favourable weather, although a little before the sides entered the field a heavy storm broke over the ' district, which certainly did not improve the attend- ance. It was to be regretted that both were weakened in one position, Hanson on the Tyldesley side and the two Bates on the Warrington side all being away from their positions behind the scrimmage. It was 3.45 When Shaw kicked off almost against a gale. Tracks were made direct for the Tyldesley line Fair Turner and Evans leading the way, and Warring- ton gave early signs of a resolute attack. Fearnley saved capitally, whilst Shaw gained a few yards by judicious kicking, a performance he repeated a few moments later. A penalty kick was taken by Fair Turner, but the attempt struck the posts below the cross-bar, and although Woodward and W. Berry dribbled away, Webster checkmated them, and Plurnptc.n eventually kicked dead. The last-named met the drop-out in clean style. The game was again waged on the home lines, Teare just missing when over the line, and Fearnley again saved. Smart play by Taylor, Shaw, and Bell gave the latter a capital chance, and when everyone had pointed to his success Webster took after him and reached him near the quarter flag, knocking him into touch. Heesom relieved slightly from a pass by Evans, and then a few sharp transfers by the same player and Lally reached the half-way flag. A stiff scrimmage here saw Donohue, Ashton, and Tears prominent parties but the home forwards persisted in the attack, and from one rush the oval was taken over the Warringten line, and W. Berry scored, Shaw failing at a difficult place. Urged on by this last success, Tyldesley again tried the rushing business, but this time Boscow met them finely, and a tine kick landed the oval on the Tyldesley line. A. Fearnley cleared the impending danger, and Berry tried a long pass to Bell, but Ffeesom floored him befe rehe could get away. Another free kick fell to Warrington's credit, and this time, being in a favourable position, Fleesom essayed the attempt, but met met with the same luck as his predecessors. Jolley, from the drop-out,made an effort, but found the opposing force just too strong, and Buff Berry, with short kicks, reached the half-way flag, Flumpton here making his mark. His drop at goal was wide of its mark, and then Ashton got over the line near the corner flag, the result of a return by Boscow, but the point being dis- puted, the home umpire was appealed to. and consequently the try was disallowed. Following this hard luck came another attack,this time Turner,Nevins, Holmes, and Evans leading the way, but Shaw saved marvellously, and a drop by the home centre reached the half-way flag. Heesom was loudly applauded for a fine tackle of J. Fearnley, and then Plurcpton tried to get in after some pretty cross dribbling by Evans, Lally, Bandies, and Nevins, but lost possession near the line. Another run by Plumpton was spoiled by an erratic pass, and Heesom tried a shot at goal with no sucoess. Boscow met the drop-nut, but Nevins was a shade too eager, for although Fearnley played the ball over the line, and Nevins secured possession, the home custodian had not been allowed his lawful five yards, and this point also was overruled. Evans was next pulled up on the line, and another minor was recorded, after fine passing by Lally, Evans, Heesom, and Webster, this latter point bringing half-time, with the score— Warrington, 0-0-5 ; Tyldesley, 0-1-0. There was a consensus of opinion that the game, so far as the result I was concerned, was as good as over, Tyldesley being in the majerity, and having a streng wind at their back. The Warringtonians, however, played up surprisingly, and direct from the kick-off gave signs of making a bold bid for honours. Turner's kick-off was aided by Bandies and Donohue, and from some capital passing Webster got clear, and when everyone had pointed to a certain scere, he dallied in his career, with the result that he was overtaken, and a glorious chance lost. The run led up to an attack on the home lines, and after Lally had failed Jolley gathered well and got over, but again was the verdict against the visitor. From a scrim- mage the Tyldesley forwards got the better of the deal, but Donohue saved daringly, and Heesom falling in an attempt to make a mark, Boscow was reached, and with his usual coolness directed the -homestere back to their quarters. Pretty passing by the Tyldesley backs was ineffective, and the game toned down at the Tyldesley quarters, the Warrington forwards playing finely together. Bandies threw across to Webster, who forced matters on the home line. A sharp pass from Berry to Shaw saw that player kicking to Webster, but no mistake was made. Berry was again penalised for his too strict attention to Lally, but some bungling of the Warrington backs gave the homesters an insight of their opponents' goal. The stay was but brief, for Jolley, Donohue, and Fair. Turner came away from the ruck, and the game was contested at half-way. It wanted telt Ave minutes from the call of time, and War- rington e ere in a minority when Lally being pressed punted to A. Fearnley, and this player being at fault, Jolley was at hand, and, forcing his way past several opponents, wound up a brilliant effort by scoring under the pests. The game was now Warrington's provided they could kick a goal, but their ill-luck stuck to them to the last, and Fieesom's kick was turned outside, and ,the final result read as a draw.

Wavrington :—J. Boscow, back ; F. Plumpton, F. Henson,. and H. Webster, three-quarters : John Evans and T. Lally, half backs ; H. Ashton, Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Nevins, W. Handles, J. Holmes, T. Donohue, J. T. Thorniley, and H. Teare, forwards. Tyldesley A. Fearnley, back ; J. Fearnley, Taylor, Shaw, and Bell, three-quarters ; J. Berry and W. Berry. half hacks ; Woodward, Sutcliffe, Tinker, Whitehead, Shepherd, Fell, A. Smith, and Worthington, forwards. WARRIKOTON " A" v. TYLDFSLRY " A."—At Warring- ton, before a goodly number of spectators, Tyldesley having lost choice of. ends started against the wind, an invasion at once being made into Warrington territory. A fine dribble by Berry, assisted by Antrobus and Hampson, carried the scene of operations to the " Bong,ers " 25, and the leather was subsequently kicked to the line. The home team seemed to have a fine chance at this stage, tint the visiting forwards quickly got together, and taking full advantage of the want of cohesion amongst their opponents, cleared the danger. A capital screw over the scrimmage by Smith found touch near the line, and .eom the following pack Bate dodged over finely, Ashurst kicking a splendid goal. After this Wilson was called upon, but he saved splendidly, and then Tyldeslev, by a series of kicks, reached the Warrington line. Here Bate started a grand dribble, and again Tyldesley were beaten back. Then Antrobus almost dribbled over, but the wretched for- ward play of the home team enabled Tyldesley to relieve. A pretty bit of passing between Bate, Smith, Barnes, and Daniels took the warfare ef the visitors' lin es.but Fearnlev dodged round a scrimmage to midfield. Then Chadwick ' intercepted a bad pass, and Warrington were pressed, until DanieLs cleared splendidly. Retaliation on the part of Miller put his side on the aggressive, but the home forwards for once in a way wheeled a plck and relieved. Long kicks between Ashurst, Wilson, and Lawless ended in play raging at the centre line, and the leather coming loose, Bate kicked away, and regaining possession, ran in a good try. The re-start saw War- rington rush down the field, forcing the ball over the line, Wilson kicking dead to save disaster. A free kick to Tyldesley was responded to by Bate, and directly afterwards the same player threw to Lawless, who effected a grand run. Here Fearnley passed to Chad- wick, who had a clear field, but nothing came at the chance. The display of the forwards was extremely

div.head: WIDNES V. RUNCORN.
div.p: WIDNES V. RUNCORN.

A great amount of interest centred in the meeting of there rival teants for the first time this season, on the Lowerhouse-lane ground, on Saturday. So far 'this season neither club have done very much, as the follow- ing record will show :--Runcorn ; Played, 7 won, 2; drawn, 2; lost, 2; points for, 16; against 20. Widnes : Played, 5.; won, 1 ; lost. 4; points for, 12; against 37 Widnesians always have given Runcorn a capital game, and the supix)rterers of the Lancashire club were very hopeful. The weather turned out fine, and about 1,000 specta- tors were present when Brennan started the game for Widnes. Crompton missed his return, but the forwards rushed the ball down to the centre line, and Brennan got in a fine kick, which Pendlebury attended to, and George Wright was prominent in breaking up the rush by Cestrians. Widnes held a slight advantage in scrim+ mages,and gradually worked their way into their oppon- ents' quarters, where Alford and Wright put in some ' good work. Rogers cleared his lines iii fine style, and Hartle% nearly let in Hughes by dallying with the ball. Falkner took a free kick on the centre line, and Brennan greatly displeased the Runcorn spectators by touching down when he could easily have put in a kick. Abrams directly afterwards forced Hartles to concede a minor, and Whelan led a rush by the home forwards, which Crompton.attended to. Barber compelled Houghton to handle for the first time, and he kicked over goal line. Johnson had to temporarily leave the field. Runcorn made an onslaught on the Widnes line and Crompton almost dropped a goal with a flying kick. Hogan transserred the play to the centre but Whines was again hard pressed, and Brompton, who was well fed by his wings,was too well watched to score, and a loud shout announced the fact that the home for- wards were careering away. Pendlebury proved the saviour of his side„ and Hartles responded to a kick by Crompton in a very feeble manner. From the line out, Alford missed a golden opportunity by failing to take Barber's pass, and Houghton put his side on the attack. Faulkner took a free kick in favourable possession, hut his attempt at goal went wide and mid-field was a scene of hostilities. Wright did yeoman service for Widnes at a critical time.and Foster pulled Crompton up under post, a very narrow shave. Alford took the ball to the centre line where numeretze scrimmages took place,. without any advantage to either team. Hogan was ordered off the field by the referee for some informality, and Widnes was left with fourteen men. Alford attended to a dangerous rush by the Cheshire team, but Rogers returned ; Taylor scored, and Crompton kicked a goal a minute before the interval arrived. Faulkner re-started the game, and Widnes rushed off' In a most determined manner. A line-out near the Run- oorn goal line ensued, and the visitors' defence had a warm time of it. Brennan had a clear run in, but was called back, and Runcorn had a turn of the pressure,. but the danger was averted by Brennan, and play settled in mid-field. Final result, Runcorn 1 goal 4 minors ; Widnes 3 minors.

Runcorn :—Hooghton, back; Rodgers, Crompton, and Pendlebury, three-quarter backs; Robinson and Abrams,. balf backs ' • Faulkner, Riley, Hughes, Taylor, Williams, Langley, Damies, Hampson, and Moores, forwards. Widnes antes, back ; Alford, Brennan, and Barber, three-quarterbacks ;Drummond and Wright, half backs ; Whelan, Gordon, Hogan, Johnson, Foster, Wynne, R dgeway, Shaw, and Fraser, forwards.

div.p: LIVERPOOL JUNIOR CUP. FIRST ROUND)

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION Y. BOOTLR AT/11,8110 Resintva.—These teams met at Sea-view. Bootle, on Saturday. T. Jones, the Warrington custodian,, was- absent owing to illness. Forbes kicked off, and an advance was made on the Bootle citadel where a strong attack was made on the home goal, Fennelly at length. passing to Norman. who drew first blood for Warring- ton ten minutes from start. The home fortvards then got away, Jones and Gibson doing a good sprint. Davies' intercepted and relieved. Fennelly now getting posses- sion raced away, and Grossing to T. Mather the latter shot wide. Play for tho next ten minutes was in mid- I field. Gill secured the sphere, failing in the final attempt, while at the other end T. Mather had a sure goal disallowed for off-side. Kincaid conceded'a corner,. nothing accruing from Gibson's place-kick,,the visitors' backs repulsing. The homesters tried hard to equalize,. but J. Mather's defensive powers, together with Davies and Kincaid, were equal to the occasion,, the whistle sounding for half-time with the score—Warrington 1 goal, Bootle O. Be-starting, the opening exchanges- were in midfield, but the homesters at length pulled them- selves together and Gibson equalized from a scrimmage. Play now became very fast, each side striving to gain the lead. After a reverse the visitors livening up, had the matter almost in their own way, T. Mather equalizi- ing from a pass by R. Fennelly, the latter scoring with. a grand shot. After an interval of midfield play, during which one of the Bootle players met with a slight acci- dent through colliding with Phillips, which,, however, did not necessitate him leaving the field,. the Warrington forwards getting pos,session raced away,. Pierpoint scor- ing No. 4. Warrington still continued to. presa severely but the whistle sounded with the score—Warruagton, 4 goals ; Bootle Athletic, 2.

i THE MURDER OF DR. KIRWAN.
A PRISONER'S ADMISSION OVERHEARD.

At Southwark Police Court, on Friday week, the four men charged with being concerned together with robbing and strangling Dr. William rater Kirwan, in Whitecross- st., London, were brought up before Mr. Lushington for further examination. Their names were given : Edward Waller (24), stoker; Henry Lee (28), stoker; Charles Balch (30), general dealer; and James Noble (25), costermanger. The court was crowded during the hearing of the case.—Mr. Sims recapitulated at some length the facts as they have already been reported. He mentioned that since the accused were last before the Court an inquest had been held on the body of the de- ceased, and the coroner's jury had returned a verdict of wilful murder against the prisoners Balch, Waller, and Noble, and had exonerated Lee from participation in the actual murder. It was not, however, his intentions to abandon the charge against that prisoner, as there now was evidence which was not called before the coroner to show that he had been seen in the company of the other prisoners on the morning of the day the. [murder was committed. Mr. Sims caused a sensation ' in the court by the announcement that he proposed to call a witness who had overheard a conversation be- tween Waller and Lee, in the reception cell at Holloway, in which Waller made a confession of having taken a prominent part in the assault,and also stated that Balch took out a knife to stab the doctor, but was prevented by him (Waller). He further stated that in preventing • Balch from using the knife he got a cut on the chin,and, . added Mr. Sims,. the fact that a blood-stained handker- , chief was in his possession, and that there was a cut on his face, was corroborative evidence of the conversation. ' —Witnesses were called to prove that the deceased was seen with a low woman, and one of them said the woman afterwards spoke to the prisoners Balch, Lee,. arid Noble, and that they tried unsuccessfully to get him to go into a common lodging-house. Subsequently they went to a public-house.—The prisoners were remanded. The police have ascertained that about a week prior to the death of Dr. Kirwan, a man naened Haynes, who on Friday was sentenced to nine months' hard labour, was arrested for a daring highway robbery in. the Borough, and during his incarceration in Holloway he was regularly visited and supplied with food by the gang now in custody for causing the death of Dr. Kirwan,. ot which .Noble, known by the soubriquet of the Ace of Spades," was the head. It appears that on October 16th, Inspector O'Dea, the chief of the Criminal Investb, gation Officers for South London, received the following letter :0—
" Eter Majksty's Nevrgate, Oct. 18, 1892. " Dear Sir,-1' think I can about clear up the Borough mystery,if you willcome and see me.—Yours truly.
JOHN FPIATIMELSTONE.
" Inspector O'Dea."

On October 18th, Mr. O'Dea,. accompanied by Detec- tive-Sergeant Gentle, went to Newgate and sought an interview with the man Featherstone, who made the following statement I am. a prisoner awaiting trial at the Central Criminal Court for felony. I was com- mitted for trial from Marlborough on October 13th, and was conveyed the same day to Benoway Prison. I was placed in theTeeeption cell with two other men. One of them told me his name was Waller, and he said, Me and this man 'meaning a man afterwards found to be Lee' 'are charged with killing a bloke,' I said,' Where' and he said, In the Borough.' I said, Whereabouts in the‘Borough,?" He said,," We.isad been drinking in A public-houser and we got the old toff boozed. We then took him up ,court. There was three of us, one man they have not got, Noble. my mate Balch, and myself. td you dolt ?' I put one of my hands in his shirt collar and the. other over his mouth, and held hint while Balch—who had got his knife out to stab him, but I atopned him, and I got a slight stab on my chin with the knife.—struck him on the head with his fist, and the other man, the one they have not got went through his clothes.' I said ." How much did you get ?' and he replied, • Only one- pound six.' I said, That is not much to kill a man for,' and he said, We did not intend' to kill him, and if we'd known he had only so little (money), like that we should not have toue.hed' him." I asked Waller what sort of a man he was, and he said ' He's an old toff ; a mouthpiece." I said,,'•What isthat ?' and he said,, • A solicitor.' I said, Did anyone see you with the olki gentleman ? " and he said, Ves,.wone luck. A, woman from the public- house where we were has identified us, but she has made a, mistake in the man (pointing to Lee.) He went into the public-house and had a half-pint, but he did not drink, with us." I'll take ten years for my chance,'. said Waller, but I said, '-You will get off ; no one saw you,do it.' Waller then said, ' There was an old woman inthe court where we took the old toff down, , and I believe-she saw us. That is sure to come up against us. Dll take 20 years for my chance. I don't care so long as-it does net come to a hanging job.'"

div.head: LIGHT FANTASTIC MADE EASY:
div.p: THE LIGHT FANTASTIC MADE EASY:

The winter season is now coming on, with its long evenings. The. hearts of our merry youth and maiden- hood, to say-nothing of those of maturer years, will be fluttering with, delight at the prospect of the dances, balls, at homes,.Cinderellas and ties long nights, whereat to "chase the glowing hours with flying feet." But alas !' What of the well flower erkl those who cannot ,danoe. Dire,vsill be the heartburning and extensive the regret at the inability to trip the light fantastic, with that graceful serenity of gliding movement which is characteristic of the experienced dancer of both sexes. Let such howsver take heart of hope. A novelty has been invented and is now being published, under the name of " Bavette's registered system of practical self- I tuition in dancing," by which it is claimed that anyone I may acquire any dance perfectly, and without aid in less than half an hour. The method by which it purposes. to -achieve this wonder is as follows : "-Eich,pupil is supplied with a stiff sheet of paper or canvas,.on which is marked out in full size the position of the feet at each step of the•dance. The movement of each foot tot s next position, is traced by a dotted h 0.,, which also indicates the pathof the foot during the step. Each footmark is numbered and lettered to shew its exact relation to the dance and the music. The pupil simply stands on the footmarks which indicate the start ing position, and traces his or her feet to their next and following positions by the dotted lines and the numbers. It will thus be seen that the pupil cannot make a mis- take. Nor is this all. Each pupil is further supplied with a complete set of written instructions, which fully explain, the music, the time;„and the steps of each dance ; . with rules for the acquisition of graceful and " good " dancing, and the avoidance of clumsy or " bad " danc- iug ; with a small doplicate of the full sized steps, which may be carried about in the pocket, and so admit of practice at any convenient opportunity; and perhaps most valuable of all, with.a Diagram of Practical Steps ' for each dance, and full, explanation of the difference between the th.oretical dance steps and the practical. movements. The latter is an immense advantage," Professor !layette's dance charts seem to have a good 'future before them. He has fixed the price of each dance at Is. 9d.—a very bow figure indeed. It is a good thing, and should be in the hands of all who would dance, and dance well,, for whose benefit we may add the information that the systems are published by the Professor himself at Salisbury Academy, Wavertree, • Liverpool.:
