THE CHARGE OF THEFT AGAINST A COMMISSION AGENT.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, be- fore Messrs. W. Long (chairman) and H. genry Atkins, commission agent, of Acton Bridge, :was, charged with stealing on the 12th inst.,.a leg ot :muttom,, value 7:4., the property of Alice Reoth, ,butcher,,stockton Heath. Mr. Jenkins defended.— Ilse prosecutor said on the day in question she hung at leg of mutton at her shop door for sale..and last saw it there about three o'clock in the alter- 'noon. About seven o'clock her. sister had) two orders for beef to deliver for her at Stretton„and witness- asked the prisoner who was passing..wieh his wife ID the shandry to give her sister a ride to Strettom. He consented, and witness handedithe two•pieces of beef to her sister in the cart, and ii wae-drisren, off. She did not miss Ihe leg of mutton until two. children told her about it being taken away in the cart. She went to Stratton, and saw P:M.Bratt there, and he met the prisoner there- his carbrand asked him if he had anything in it that did not belong to him, and he said he had not. Brett searched the cart, and found it at the prisoner's feet under the straw and the hook in it. She identified biy the peculiar way her brother dressed the meate—By Jenkins :: When Atkins stopped at her door and when. the constablesaw him he was sober. He had dealt with her once ortwice during two or three years.—Jarnes- 'Etarwaker„aged 11, said about 7 o'clock on the evening. Of the 121hinst., he saw Atkins take the leg of mutton 'and put it in his cart at the back. He told Mrs. Booth about it after Mr. Atkins had driven off.: with , hen sister.—By Mr. Jenkins: There were other children a bout,, and he did not take the iog secretly, He was.not tipsy,. but had had drink.—By Police-Superin- tendent Atherton : The movement of taking the leg was note one.—Ethel Churchill, aged 11,. said she was with Annie Hughes another little girl, close to tile shop and saw the prisoner take a leg of mutton from the shop &or and throw it into the cart, and after- wards told Mina Booth.—By Mr. Jenkins: He did net do. It in a cunning,' way, but quite openly.—P.C. Brett deposed to receiving information from Mrs. Booth about 6.45p.rn.,,0n the 19th inst., at Stretton, and therealnd- ing a leg of mutton in the cart under the seat in.froat. He charged the prisoner with stealing it, and he said I " I never took,it, at least, I cannot remember it. Next:: morning when washing himself he said " I tell you tha,. lam a ruinedonan over this. lain well known imLaie- cashire and Cheshire, and people will never look on me the Caine after this."—By Mr. Jenkins : He had oad drink, but could walk straight. Witness had known him as a respectable man. He took him into the house and gave him IL eup of tea and something to eat.—Mr. Jenkins : Very good of you.—ln further cross-examina- tion witness said+ the leg of mutton was not wrapped up in any way.—The prisoner was then forinelly charged,and pleaded not guilty,choosing to be dealtwith summarily.--Mia Jenkins addressed the court for the defence. Hesnict the prisoner had always conducted himself as an honourable man, and if he were convicted he would undoubtedly be practically ruined from a coin. mercial point'of view. On the day in question, he had driven into Warrington with his wife and unfortunately, visited several: publiehouse.s, returning much intoxir cated ; and whiih in this state actuated by some extra- ordinary impule,, unhung the leg of mutton, and put iO into his cart: There was no attempt to hide it. Was it contrary to ordinary experience, that a man suffering from the effects of drink, when meat was being removed from the shopitito,a cart, as in this case, should, though - lessly, in the muddled state of his brain, unhook,a leg cf. mutton, and put it in also? Could the Bench believe that in the presence of the children standing about, anl considering that the sister of the owner of theieg at mutton was in the cart he would be such a madlool.rie to take it and. pat it in the cart, with the deliberate.in tention of stealing it? He submitted that there was net the slightest semblance of criminal intent. The moment he was charged by the constabbe, he said "-II cannot remember it," and next morning, rousing him- self ftom his drunken thoughts, what did he say,. ":Why if this be true, I am., a .ruineall man.' Might he not have thought in his .hwy. eindition,, that his wife had bought the leg, of mutton,, and thrown it into the cart ?. There waa-ao ' indicationof criminal intent.—John Marsey, stablen:an, deposed to the prisoner being drunk, but not very drunk, at 6:30' taco:, on the 12th inst.—Miss Millington, , Booth's sister, deposed that Mrs. Watkins asaistea. her with her basket of meat into the cart. lir. Dutton gave him a similar tharacten—The Bench having considered the case 7.rivately faro semi ten minutes, the Chairman, on their return, said they were of.opinion that he took the mutton, but waa riot in a fit state to be conscious of what he was do:ag, and were,opitewilling to give him therkenefit of thedoubt. The sentence was that he come up, for jiidginants when calledlupon, but the Bench did tee want to. ta:lna away his oharacter. and if he would on make up Ne-mind to put nomore into his mouth thao which made a fool of .hirmand made him unconscious-4X what ho was doing, he would hear no more about the matter. Yaw it was not necessary for men to drink a order to get eustomers, as it formerly was. There were lots of men whocarried ona.respectabie business and weer touched drink, , and hehoped this case would be a sufficient warning to him. to be determined not to take- drink again. Sir,—The impression one gets from reading the report in your paper of the licenses granted at the Sessions, on Thursday, the 20th, is that I applied on behalf of the Young Iden's Christian Association for a music and dancing license, whereas I applied for and received a music license only, and not dancing.—Yours, W. H. BAYLEY.

div.head: "NATIONAL EVIL"
div.p: A "NATIONAL EVIL"

Sir,—May 1 be allowed through the medltim of your valuable columns to place before the ratepayers,the way in which they are represented, or fail to las represented in the councils of the town. Though only a small minority of the ratepayers are members of either 'political association, yet the political associations, select end return representatives to the Town Council. This arises from the indifference of many, the political , Intolerance of others, and the local ambition of many public men. It is a proverbial saying that misfortunes never come sirgly, the reason being that one misfortune has a tendency to cause another. So likew;se one evil often brings into existence others, and the error of mak- ing municipal elections political has spread throughout the country, producing cliqueism, and fostering narrow views, by whir'. means public life is too often degraded 10 the attainment of selfish purposes and ambitious ends. Yet it is the duty of every one of us, whatever be our politics, religion, or position, tl regard as sacred the public good, and to prevent its being trampled upon not only by violence and crime, but also by the un- scrupulous pursuit and endeavour to obtain poJitions of prominence, honour, and praise. I must now leave the subject, at least for a tiale, in hope that others who have more time and ability than myr.2lf, will help to overcome this serious naticnal evil .—Yours, &c. S. KENYON. Warrington, Octobot 27th, 1892.

div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC.

Sir,—lt should be a standing disgrace to the town ef Warrington that an epidemic of smallpox should gain such alarming proportions, without the Sanitary Authorities (seemingly) having the power of grappling with it in a -satisfactory manner. What has been the effect of plac- ing the hospital in Dallatn-lane ? Why, after a strong westerly wind across Winwick-road, a serious, and apparently severe outbreak of the disease has occurred in that district, 3 deaths already reported, and a large number taken to the hospital. I am certain that not sufficient care is taken in guarding an infected house. I think a sanitary official should l. left in charge for at least two days, to prevent curious and sympathizing neighbours from entering the house. But the most serious question is : " Are the Sanitary Authorities really trying to put a stop to the epidermic, or are they doing their best to spread this loathsome disease all over the town? I sometimes come to the batter conclusion, especially when I see a soil cart stand- ing outside or near an infected house and perhaps a dozen children playing arouna it, to say nothing about passers by, who are sure to get an unsavoury sniff. I say: Stop these disgusting vehicles at once from parading our streets in the day time. Why this work cannot be done at night I cannot conceive; neither can I understand who could possibly object to its being done at night. Again, why not send a staff of men over the town with carts distributing chloride of lime to those people who are too careless or perhaps too lazy to obtain it them- selves. The idea seems to be that the inhabitants should look after these matters and take care of them- selves, and quite right too if they would only do so ; nut failing their doing so. the Sanitary Committee should see that it is done ; also seeing that all dwellings are in a proper sanitary condition and disintectants supplied where necessary. Then, I think, all courts, alleys, and yards in the town should be well whitewashed, at least twice a year, this work to be done by the Sanitary Committee and the landlords of the property charged with cost of same. Finally, the inhabitants should at once demand that proper provision should be made for any future epidemics, by erecting a hospital of sufficient size, some distance outside the town.—Yours truly, ALFRED LLOYD.

div.head: SAGE OF' PENKETH IN A FURY.
div.p: THE SAGE OF' PENKETH IN A FURY.

Sir,—lt is instructive and amusing to watch the Sage of Penketh wax wrathful, until eventually his wrath bursts into a fury. In doing so, one can scarcely fail to note the mighty difference between the Sage of Plato and the modern Agnostic, the Sage of Penketh. The former, in consequence of a severe and life-long discip- line, subjected all his passions to reason, the complete mastery of which finally enabled him to live a divine life, and to enjoy sweet and blissful communion with the immortal gods. In striking and appalling contrast to this highly-faveured individual, the Sage of Penketh starts forth into the field of battle, and plunging into the thickest of the fight, brandishes aloft his shillelagh, challenging whoever ventures across his path, and is prepared to enter into fierce and sanguinary soirflict with a " goose," with all his readiness of resoarce. However, the sage of Penketh is fallible, and corn- mite himself again and again to fatal inconsistencies. " All living creatures " he says " have one invaluable and irreplaceable possescion, life." True, very true, oh ! sage of Penketh! But this statement makes your difficulties all the " more serious." For if man, along with the lower animals, shares the same invaluable and irreplaceable possession how can man be justified in taking away lit.) at all ? Man has no right in consequence to kill even the vermin which infect his garden or his nightcap. In addition, I repeat an objection I formerly raised. If the sage of Penketh links man on to the lower animals by means of immutable and neces- sary laws, then why should not the inmates of asylums be put to death in consequence of the struggle for existence and the survival of the fittest. It is scarcely credible that the sage of Penketh would write the following,:sentencet—"The agnostic does not take upon himselt to judge as to who is and who is not so fitted" (for life) ; " he is content to leave our com- mon mother to do that, and she does it very effectually. It is the natural savage man who thus assumes nature's prerogative. But the study of nature is the spccial pro- vince of science. Accordingly Mr. Peers would exclude from such study the cultured man of the 19th century and fling the study of nature into the hands of the sav- age. When the successor of the sage of Penketh appears upon the scene he will find it difficult to improve upon this. Yours, Szc. October 26th, 1892.

div.head: LEARNER.
div.p: A LEARNER.
THE EIGH r _HOURS QUE sTioN.

Sir,—Your correspondent, R. Sto tisy, has returned to of the charge, and what are the we ipons his warfare? First, a couplet of doggerel and' ,he slang" eight bob a day."lle has changed his tune,b, At what does he mean by 4ght • eight bob ?" If he means e• shillings why not say so Ana don on this eight hours ? I have asked for info eight hours, and who are to question. Who are to wor xticulars, but R. Storey deals in work longer? Iwt pa what he can to disparage me by generalities, and does ing to make it appear that I am falseop poserde representation, teai gtihotn sours day for miners and others; and when • I ask for i' aformation he says I shut my eyes. Why does he not e Alighten them with the information I ask for instead oI abusing one by false inuendoes ? He assumes tco r/inch with regard to " Cymro " and his class, and w'aat does he know of me and my class? bs .othing ; and yet he poses as an oracle. He Aisonoaluoteiltyd rose wise men who" rush where angels fear to tread." If he is so anxious for a legal eight hours day for miners and others, let him convert the Durham colliers and the railway workers, and then point to something tangible that he has done, but they won't have his logic. 1 care not a straw to what point the working hours may be reduced if it will be a benefit to the working classcs. I shall share in it, and ' I dare assert that I have doe more for the shortening of the hours of labour than ever he has with all his impudent assumption and his raving about my opposing others less fortunate than myselt in obtaining shortened hours. I believe I know as much of the ten hours Act and the necessity for it and the good it has done as ever R. Storey did. I need no quotations from Carlyle Ruskin, or Thorold Rogers, or any advice from R. Carlyle, on any of the labour or land questions or political problems advocated by the advanced Radicals of the day. Your paper has published many a letter from my pens on these ques- tions, and life being spared, and if you kindly permit, it will again. As to his advice to me to read more and study deeper, he is a great man for deep study—l have read his letters, and my study of them has been that they are a farrago of unmeaning platitudes, a raving against wealth and wealthy people, and " the base E s. d." and yet he expects when his millennium comes to get "eight bob a day." I should like to see it,only I fear I shall not live long enough. This would-be political prophet and doggerel poet tells me to study nature and the signs of the times. Ido so without his meddlesome advice, which 1 treat with contempt ; and the signs of the times are so pain" that he who runs may read " One sign is this. We have had a cold spring followed by a cold ungenial summer. We have had short crops and a bad harvest. Of 69 summers in my life the last has been the most unfavourable. These things bring about aglicultural and com- mercial depression and scarcity of labour which means poverty more or less all round, and which no legal enactment can remove. Anothsr sign of the times is foreigners from all the civilized countries of the world coming to England, to London, to Man- chester, to Bolton, to Oldham and other towns. Sharp, Stewart, and Co., Byer and Peacock, and Co., taught them to build locomotives. They gave high wages, these forcigners, to our best men to go and instruct their men, and now they build their own and want none of ours, but compete with us in every market. Another sign of the times is, the machinists of other towns have made machinery for all the work for the production of cotton goods, and other textile fabrics. Our skilled mechanics have gone out with the machines, and taught their men how to make similar machines. Our spinners and weavers have gone—skilful and trustworthy men—and taught the natives how to do as they did, and they were apt learners, and now they are our competitors, produc- ing what we produce, and underselling us in our own markets, working 72 hours a weAt for a far less wage than our people earn, and living on food that does not cost half what the food we consume costs. These are "signs of the times," Mr. Storey, that all your rant, backed with doggerel verse, cannot get over. The [poverty problem has to be met and met in in this coun- try. itherica will not have our emigrants unless they have money. The kb:olr market there is overstoCkOr and in Australia It Is a drtig, The pot about Amara and stale pulpit platitudes are eaply ri.d%uious. Poll Warrington, taking every trade in it, by a fair ballot for or against a legal eight hours day, and it will condemn its being made compulsory by law. Combination can secure it, trades unions can if they wish ; notwithstand- ing that Mr. Storey tries to make me say they could not, said nothing of the kind, and to say I did is simply false—l say they wont go to Parliament for what they can do for themselves. I hope Mr.Storey will come out with some tangible scheme when next he writes, expres- sed in reasonable common sense, free from the rant of his former epistles.—l am, sir, yours respectfully, CYMRO. October 24th, 1892.

div.head: "LEGAL EIGHT HOURS FOR MINERS."
div.p: "LEGAL EIGHT HOURS FOR MINERS."

Sir,—Let me say one word as to " Cymro's " last letter. It was inhuman, where he went in for mothers not suckling their children, not watching over them in sickness, or soothing them when crying, or putting them to bed, all of which are involved in his eight hours work- ing day for mothers and wives. His comparison is thoughtless and unnatural. Where he opposes an eight hours day for men, he is running his head against a wall in his cant about domestic servants, Zsc. If men obtain lan eight hours day, then toiling woman would also. Think deeper? " dymro " says "our neighbours and competitors over the water, work twelve hours a day." But Jack's master, formerly made English Jack work fifteen, or sixteen hours a day. In 1817. Robert Owen, appears to have made an effort to revive the eight hours system that existed in the fifteenth cen- tury. But before the reign of Elizabeth ended, artisans and labourers had sunk into a worse condition of long hours, &c., "than anything which obtained in the four- teenth and fifteenth centuries," the working week, about the end of the seventeenth century, consisting of 72 hours. Are we so simple and foolish, as" Cymro " evidently shows himself to be, when be writes about us " getting more lazy than we formerly were," and our neighbours over the water working twelve hours a Jay," &c.? an we shut our eyes to the fact that with our shorter working hours, England is still the richest empire in the world.and English working-men, (woman and children) are blessed by legal shortening of hours . - . .

effected by Union Leaders (scorned by " Cymro ") our German. &c., neighbours, to whom "Cymro "doubtless refers, still working too long? Not ruin but blessing has hitherto followed every Act of Parliament, shortening the hours of labour. If the proof of the pudding be in the eating, then " Cymro " can have his fill of his own pudding, which he makes of such stuff as follows: "A legal eight hours day. The much-talked of and more written of subject upon which much wind.ink,and paper have been wasted." Yes, most certainly !by such as "Cymro," I, as a minor, must Inve been a very dull, unthinking, scholar. if I know nothing about miners in Lancashire, &c., having during 40 years, or a little more, repeatedly tried to secure an eight hours working day by trades union effort, but never having succeeded for any length of time. " Cymro " says " seven hours of hard work is quite enough, and to follow it up anywhere. I could do with six. Underground it is more than enough, in a hot and coal-laden atmosphere." If" Cymro "can do, or say anything to prevent miners, &c., obtaining a legal eight hours, we see how true and brave a Briton " Cymro" has proved himself to be, by attacking from his hiding place a measure which the

. . . . vast ma7 jonty of miners now demand: as proved at the late General Elections, by the rejection of such colliery masters as Col. Blundell of the Ince division, and secur- ing one of the most notable vict•ries at the election for Mr. Samuel Woods, nainers'agent,and by reducing Sir F. S. Powell Bart's majority of 1885 from 519 to 110 in 1892, and thus in Tory Wigan, all but, petting their agent, Mr. rhos. Aspinall, in. And even noble honest John Morley, whom I should have regretted losing his seat at Newcastle-on-Tyne, only managed to keep his seat be- cause of his other many excellent quaiities. But Mr. J. Craig lost his seat ? The legal eight hours question did it. These stern facts prove, that at least, miners by a large majority believe in fighting for, and ought to speedily have given to them a legal eight hours. If as " Cymro " must admit, miners health renders it needful, that they should not work more than eight hours during any one day in the mine ; and this should be secured by Trade Onion efforts only. He ought to un- derstand a little more of human nature—that (1) There cannot be a sound mind in an overworked, unhealthy body. (2) That a sound mind is essential to compre- hending and discharging the social, moral, and spiritual duties of mankind. (3) Therefore when workisg-men are overworked and languid, too many of them in hope of throwing off the feeling of exhaustion at the week's end swallow " the thief that steals away their brains " causing a mere poisonous titillation of their dying nerves, leading alas to such sad explosions in coal mines on Monday morning, &c. " Cymro" has utterly failed to properly comprohend the final Cause of such is the old heathenish blind, and base love of :2 s d, more than the bodies and souls of men. "Was ever man the better" Ruskin profoundly asks " for having coffers full of gold ?" But who can measure the guilt that is in- curred to fill them ? Can " Cymro I cannot. But masters such as eat toe fat, clothe themselves with the wool, but feed not the flock." Thank God that we have many good men among all these classes who do not ignore as "Cymro " does, the good that Parliameht has done, in shortening the hours labour, &c., from the Tudor period and reign of Queen Elizabeth on to the triumph won by Lord Ashley (after- wards Lord Shaftesbury) over John Bright. Szc., with respect to the Ten Hours Bill, In 1878 the Factory and Workshop Act confirmed the statutory week at 54 hours n textile factories. During the debate on the Ten Hours Sir James Graham, Mr. Cardwell. and Mr. John Bright all contended in the House of Commons that wages would fall 25 per cent. All this was false. sicyrnro," think deeper! in 1859 Mr. Robert Baker, having then had a long ex- perience as a, factory inspector, stated in his report to the Local Science Association that, "Although the hours of work have been very much diminished, wages have increased, in some cases, forty per cent., and generally about twelve per cent. , "Cymro "is on the wrong line Let him think deeper before writing again.—Yours. &c., R. STOREY.
Warrington, October 11th, 1892.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1892 WARRINGTOS TEMPERANC
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1892 WARRINGTOS TEMPERANC

FEDERATION. ALLIANCE MEETING AT THE CO-OPERATIVE HALL. MR. W. S. CAINE, M.P., SPEAKS. A large publie meeting was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Sankey-st., on Wednesday night, under the auspices of the Warrington Temperance Federa- tion. The subject of the gathering was to support the United Kingdom Alliance. Mr. W. S. Caine M.P., was the chief speaker of the evening. The chair was taken by Mr. E. J. Guest, J.r., who was supported by the Revs. J. J. Langham, John Yonge, T. Ross; Councillor Henry Roberts and Messrs. Wm. Roberts (sec.), E. Boreland, It. Garnett, J.P., S. B. Stringer, Beswick, Pigot, Storey, Price, Thornton, Taylor (Court Missionary). Communications were received from the following gentlemen regretting their unavoidable absence :—The 1 Rev. Charles Clay, Congregational Minister of Lymm,the Rev. Ed. Reed, of the Bold-st., Emmanuel Church, Alderman Platt, and Mr. John Walker,of the Examiner. ' The latter explained that he had been confined to the house with illness for several days.

The CHAIRMAN said the question of temperance, which they were there that night to discuss, was one surrounded by difficulties of every character. The Rev. Charles Garrett had said the other day that the two great difficulties under which temperance suffered were self-interest on one hand, and inch& rence on the other. They had the self-interestedness on the part of the pub- licans and brewers, and the indifference on the pal t of the British public. That indifference was the more fatal of the two. If they had the people on their side, they would be able to gain that mastery over the publi- cans and brewers which it was the object of the United Alliance to achieve. The evils of excessive drunkenness so prevalent in the British Isles was admitted on every hand. The cause of the excessive drinking on the part of the English people was a question upon which the opinions of people differed ; and in the remedies con- sidered necessary to adopt, they had also differences of opinion. But it was not his duty that evening to go into that phase of the question. What be had to say was that as a temperance worker, he could state that the excessive drunkenness of the British people was one of the chief reasons of the diminution and fall in the trade and commerce of the empire. Other people gave other reasons for their commercial decline, and they said that the exhaustion of commercial resource had a great deal to do with it. But he did not think that was so. If the British people were a sober p ple, if they were always industrious, if they confron d their drinking evils bravely, if they spent their money upon things which they needed—in household and personal necessities— then there would be no crying out of a decline of Bri- tish commerce and trade. (Applause.) There was no necessity for him to dilate upon the sufferings and crime and privations of domestic life which were entailed by the excessive use of intoxicating liquors. They were phases of the driak curse which were universally recog- nised. They knew that if it was not for their drink one half of the police could be dispensed with ; that nine- tenths of the prisons could be done away with ; crime would be considerably diminished ; their hospitals weuld be of very little service, and asylums would only be kept for the exclusive use of a select few. But, he would ask what was the cause of all the evils which they had to contend against ? Some people said that the climate of England was such as to compel people to take stimulants. They (the temperance people) did not believe that. They believed that pecple could live in their climate without the slightest necessity for stimulants. There were other people who brought torth the more reasonable explana- tion, that the British people were, to a great extent, Suffering, from an heriditary tendency to drinking, lie believed that was sot Our ferefathers were men set,. 11:"/.. teen' urinkers ; and he was afraid that the evil habits of their ancestors were falling to their chil- dren. There was no doubt that the children of drunk- ards were much more easily led into evil ways than the children of temperate parents. (Applause.) What were the remedies which were proposed to meet these evils? When they talked about remedies they had to take into consideration the manner in which they would have to end one of the greatest evils, and that was the evil of bad associations. They found that for the most part the associations of the intemperate people were formed in the public-houses. When they talked about putting an end to public-houses they were immediately informed that they were interfering with the liberty of the subject. They would at once say that the temperance party had no right to coerce or force the people into their cause. They contended that there should be " a fair field and no favour," and they could not make men sober by Act of Parliament. That was, a very plausible argument ! They did not wish to interfere with the liberty of the people; but what they did wish to do was to curtail some of their licentiousness, or to see that their liberty was not turned into licentious- ness. The law stepped in and interfered in that character of vice. When a drunkard could not take care of himself, he was taken care of by the policeman. Their opponents said they had no right to make slaves of the British public. They did not want to do so. What ' they wanted to do, was to prevent people from making slaves of themselves, and of their wives and children. The speaker, in concluding pointed out that Parliament, whilst it certainly did not yet legislate for total abstin- ence certainly drafted its laws so as to prevent exces- sive drunkenness. The very fact that free trade in drink was not allowed, was a proof of that. The Gothenberg system, which the Bishop of Chester and Mr. Chamberlain had both agitatad for was becoming a popular measure, and, although, it was not what the Alliance aimed at,he had no doubt the system would be a great acquisition to them. (Applause.) The Rev. J. J. LANGHAM proposed the foltowing reso- lution :—" That this meeting, while thankfully recog- nising in the present increased demand for limitation of the sale of intoxicating liquors a deepened interest in temperance legislation, yet is nevertheless profoundly convinced that the history and results of all past legisla- tion in regard to the liquor traffic, abundantly prove that it is impossible satisfactorily to limit or regulate a system so essentially mischeivous in its tendencies ; and this meeting declares that no measure can meet the necessities of the nation which does not include the Direct Popular Local Veto." He fully endorsed the principle of the resolution. He was one that fully believed that the drink curse could never be fully abolished until the abolition of intoxicants was brought about. But for all that he could not attempt to say that if a majority of the people were agreed upon merely causing a limitation to the sale, he should oppose it. On the contrary, it would meet with his warm support. As a proof of that, he wished to express his warm approval of the Bishop of Chester's proposal to introduce the Gothenberg system. (Applause.) Councillor iffsesur ROIXERTS seconded the resolution. In doing so he said that the United Kingdom Alliance had been voted a nuisance by the Liberal party in many instances, because of its progressive programme. But he considered their question of temperance reform was an eminently satisfactory one. (Hear, hear.) He was a Liberal himself. He was a Home Ruler, and wanted to see Home Rule; he was a Nonconformist and wanted to see disestablishment ; and he would like to see a great measure forland reform. But he would be pleased to wait until his hair turned white, or until his head became as bald as a billiard ball—(laughter)—if he could see the ultimate attainment of a solution to the temperance question,even if it came before the other political reforms he hsd mentioned. He believed in the maxim of the late Mr. Jhn Bright "'Frost in the people," and he was con- vineed that the people would sooner or later remove the terrible evils under which they suffered. But the people had first to get the power. Ile asked them if it was reasonable to think,that if ths people in certain districts had the power to enforce their principles against the brewers, that such a thing as the recent granting of the two extra licenses would have occurred? (" No, no.") He thought that the system of licensing ought to be re- medied, se that the ratepayers could give force to their objections before an impartial tribunal. He considered that there should be more stringent laws passed upon the licensing question. It was true that the law did put certain limits on the sale of drink. But those laws were not obeyed or carried out properly. In Warrington alone, he did not think there was one license-holder who did not act with illegality for the purpose of increasing his profits ; and if these men were to be kept to the strict letter of the law (which was necessary) their , establishments would have to be watched by the police morning, noon, and night. And even then. he believed, .the law would be evaded. During some remarks upon the consequences of the liquor trade, the speaker men- tioned that the Mayoress had recently opened a sub- scription for the Life Boat Fund. The institution was a noble one, and the Mayoress' action was exceedingly praiseworthy. People were assisting it heartily, for it was stated that every year 700 lives were lost in the wrecks. Yet it was strange that that object should be taken up with so much vigour by people who would not raise a finger to save any of the 60,000 poor souls who died annually at their own doors, from intemperance. (Applause.) MR. CAINE'S SPEECH. Mr. W. 5. CAINE, who was loudly applauded on ris- ing, said he rose with very great pleasure indeed to sup- port a resolution which had been moved and seconded in such an able and statesmanlike manner, by the preced- ing spearcers. The resolution really put into a nutshell , the exact position of the temperance movement at the Present moment, with regard to its legislative aspect. There was no doubt that within the last year or two, the conscience of the nation had been roused with regard to the terrible evils that flowed from drinking and drunken. ness, has it had never been roused before, and it w.:s their business as extreme temperance reformers, to thank God, and take courage that they found such a clear manifestation of the spread of the leaven that they had been distributing throughout the country for so mans- years past. (Applause.) They in thaemeetins, were not licensing reformers, that was, not their busi- ness ; they did not believe in it, they were prohibition- ists. (Hear, hear.) Re believed in total abstinence for the individual and prohibition for the state iRe LI

nothing to do with the first part of his creed that night; what he had to do with was prohibition for the state. They stopped at nothing short of prohibition ; thvy took everything that travelled in this direction, but they did not propose schemes of licensing reform ; they left that to others. The whole problem that hail tobe solved by the 'licensing ieformex was this, how .a Man could obtain a reasonable supply of intoxicating
Liquors, without demoralizing the community. Thii problem once solved, they were all licensing reformers. It had been the fashion, and was still. to throw upon _ _ .

temperance men, the responsibility of dealing with .the liquor traffic. If there was an evil existing in the state it was incumbent upon every good citizen to4eal with it; it was not the exclusive privilege of any section of the community, but, if any section of the cotnmunity was called upon snore than another, to deal with the evil, it was that section that called it into existence. What
. _ were the evils which temperance and licensing reformers recognised as flowing from intoxicating liquors? We had a million of paupers, and a million more to take

their places. Did they And these millions of paupers I amongst the seven millions of teetotallers ? Not one. We had 300.000 jail birds in this country,and tnere were another 300,000 ready to come in. Where did they find them ? Did they find them in the ranks of the total abstainers? Yes when they were in jail—but at no other time. (Loud laughter.) So he might go through all the terrible evils that infested society, as the result of drink and drunkenness, and they found none of them among the total abstainers. Who amongst the drinkers were responsible for these evils. Was it the drunkard? No ! Study the licensing laws and you would find that no Act of Parliament had ever been passed that contemplated the supplying of drink to drunken persons. Take some low district of a great city where there were 20 or 30 liquor shops, and supposing a man came before tho magistrates, say the Warrington Bench, and said "Gentlemen, I am in a most drunken neighbourhood. I want a license for a public-house. There are 20 other licensed public-houses there. You will find these crowded to suffocation with the drunkards of the district, and they want you to license a fresh house for their accommodation." Why, even the Warrington Bench would order him out in the custody of a pcdiceman. (Laughter.) The magistrates did not create licenses to supply drunkeh persons. One of the clauses of the contract of the State with a pub- .. . .

lican, through the magistrates was, that he should not sell drink to drunken persons. In Liverpool there were 25,000 persons charged in one year with being drunk and disorderly, and only three publicans were fined for having drunken men on their premises—they got it somewhere else than at the public-house. (Laughter.) Everybody knew that the moral sense of this country was so strong that if no one went to a peblic-houses but the drunkards they would be closed to-morrow. They existed for the moderate drinker. They called them in- to existence and it was their business, not that of the temperance party, to devise licensing schemes by which they could get their drink without demoralising the community. It was very cemmon to say that the tem- perance people obstructed legislation,and the" Speaker," an intellectual organ of the Liberal party, called upon them to abandon their opposition to a licensing scheme. But the" Speaker" had reproduced a leading article that appeared 25 years ago in the " Leeds Mercury" the editor of which then was the present editor of the "Speaker." They would not have his ideas then, and because he had been busy and wanted to hash up an old article, that was no reason why they should pay attention to it now, and abandon their principles on the very edge of victory, after 53 years of battle. (Loud applause.) He said they obstructed every proposal for temperance reform, for the last 20 years. He (Mr. Caine) asked him in his own columns to give a list •.f the measures they had obstructed. He said unhesitatingly that every measure that had been brought forward in Parliament and every Act passed to restrict and limit the power of the licror trade, had been initiated and brought into law by the temperance party. (Applause.) In support of this statement, the speaker cited measures, and proceeded to say that if there was any one scandal more than another that wanted dealing with by politicians, it was the con- duct of the kublicans and the liquor trade towards the electorate ot this country, during the recent general election. It was a scandal against which every good man cried out ; and they had been expecting the present Government to give notice of their intention to bring in a bill to deal with this question. He was at the last short session that took place, and he failed to find on the list at measures and resolutions, to be introduced, any for temperance reform to be brought forward by those who accused the temperance party of obstruction. Had the Government of the day nut down a proposal to close public-houses during elections? Nothing of the sort. Had the moderate drinkers the reasonable and sensible licensing reformers done so ? No. It was there, but it , stood in his name. (Applause.) All this rot that was talked by the " Speaker " and the supporters of its views about the temperance party opposing temperance legis- lation, was absolutely false. He had no patience sv,.,h the editor of a paper like the "Speaker " sitting down and writing such rubbish as that. Mr. Caine defended the temperance party from the charge of having pre- vented the Bruce Bill being passed, showing that they had promoted it. He pointed out that the Alliance did not want imperial prohibition, but that Parliament should give to localities power to dc.l w;th +he ILiunr trade, as they had given them to deal with other matters. He condemned the Gothenburg system because though it reduced the number of public-houses, it, by devoting the profits of the liquor trade to reduction of rates, made the ratepayers participators in, and interested in sustaining, the trade. He asserted that in America where the principle had been adopted in places where prohibition did not exist, though the number of public-houses had been much reduced the condition ot things was as grave and serious as when there were twice or three times the number. He cited a number of statistics in proof of his contention. The results of drunk- enness. he urged, would be precisely the same whether the drink was sold under the Gothenburg scheme or not, whether the public-houses were licensed by the County Council or the magistrates. If you were to turn Ches- ter Cathedral into a public-house, and put the Bishop of Chester there as a publican, the results would be the same. (Laughter and applause.) The speaker referred to the allocation of what he called the " whisky money" by the County Councils among various districts, as for instance for technical education in Warrington. He pointed out that if the direct veto were obtainel, and it were exercised, Warrington would be placed in this position that it would be asking for public-houses to be closed, and then asking people to do without technical education, because of the money for it being derived from the drink trade. This would not be a nice cry to go to the ratepayers with. Be was going to propose to the Government to put into the consolidated fund all this whisky money, instead of allocating it to districts, and then give a grant in aid for the required purposes, untainted with this whisky taint. The State was already tainted with the liquor trade ; let it remain tainted, but let the ratepayers be kept clear of the taint. Mr. Caine mentioned that the municipal elections in Manchester at present were turning almost upon the one question of whether a licence should he granted to a music hall. He asked when they had the Prime Minister and the whole Government, and a majority in Parliament, pledged to the principles of the Alliance were they at the bidding of the " Speaker" to give them up? He showed that the principle of direct veto was no new one, I but already applied as to free libraries and in other ways. He observed that no one would be allowed to have a pigstye im mediately behind Sankey-st.; though plate glass was put in the stye, and it was made most artistic, and an electric light provided to see the pig by. (Laughter.) He applied the analogy to public-houses, and said he would rather live next door to a pigstye, than a public-house. (Laugh- ter.) He alluded amidst applause, to the support given to the temperance cause by Mr. William Crosfield, M.P., and expressed the opinion that next year, or the year after, the power of direct veto would be given. A machine would be put down in the midst of Warring- ton, but Warrington ould have to find the steam and fuel. They had a bie job before them, but the power given them would be the greatest means of agitation and conviction the temperance party ever had placed in their li*mds. The speaker concluded amidst much applause. The resolution was put, and carried unanimously. The Rev. JOHN YONGE proposed the following resolution :—"That this meeting rejoices at the return to Parliament of a number of mem- bers pledged to vote for the principle of direct veto, and earnestly urges upon the Government the imperative necessity of their passing into law at an early date a measure giving to the rate- payers a direct veto power over the issue and renewal of all licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquors in their respective localities. And this meeting hereby pledges itself to support the Government in their efforts to secure to the people—this power of protecting them- selves from the liquor traffic, and its consequences." Mr Yonge congratulatel Mr. Guest as one of the local magistrates on being in the chair. Ho was, he said, exceedingly anxious :hat the Warrington magistrates in- terested in temperarre reform should have at all times the courage of their convictions. There seemed to be a kind of notion that the magistrate who hap- pened to be a total abstainer should as being an extreme mar, modestly take a back seat on certain public occasions. That was a very great mistake. (Cries of" Hear, hear.") He ought to be in evidence in the orough court whenever licensing matters happened to be to the fore—(applause)—and give his vote, fearlessly, according to his convictions, because 'they did not find extreme men on the other side exercis- ing any modesty at *II. (Laughter.) He was very glad to see one or two of their new justices at the meeting. They expected a greet deal from these gentlemen. (Hear, hear.) They looked to them to deliver them so far as they possibly could from the state in which they had been living so long.to try to prevent the community from hein,g any loiger victimised by wealthy firms, and fresh lie...ses being given to districts where penple did not wantthem. They looked to the new magis- trates to prevent tte defeat of the police in their action against, publicans phere the evidence was against them. He thought in all awl] actions the Town Clerk ought to presecute—(hear, lear)—as was the case elsewhere. Mr. E. BORELAID seconded the motion, which was put, and carried pith acclamation. Mr. W. ROBESTS proposed, and the Rev. 'l'. Ross seconded, a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Mr. Ross

div.head: IRISII NA.TIONAL LEAGUERS
div.p: IRISII NA.TIONAL LEAGUERS
THE .*AItRINGTON- LIBERAL PARTY.
At the League Hall, on Tuesday night, a large number of Irishmen met under the auspices of the Irish National League. The primary object of the . . . .
meeting had been to consider' the attitude of the Irish ratepayers respecting the municipal contests
which we're 'to I:a.ve taketipluco.
But .Owing to the

compromise arrived at by tne two political parties the same day, the meeting were unable to carry their object out. After some private discussion amongst themselves, they decided to make the ob- ject _of the meeting " the criticism of the actions of . .
the Liberal party." Mr. Felix Loughlin.waa in the
chair, and he was supported by Messrs. M. Lyons, J. Lyons, B. Kean, D. Donnellan, E. Whitehead, and J.
- Byrne. Councillor Flood was also present at the
meeting as a Bpectator. The Chairman's first observations described how the

meeting was to have passed the following resolution had the municipal contests taken place :—" That we, the Irish Electors, in public meeting assembled, desire to state that it is our determination at the approaching Municipal Elections, to remain perfectly neutral, and neither by work or vote to support either political party, and we call upon our people in every ward of the Borough to loyally abide by this resolution." The contests,he said were not going to take place. The political parties declared that it was on account of the small-pox . . . .

epidemic. Anyhow, it was "an ill wind which biew nobody good," for although the epidemic was not con- ferring any benefits on the town it was getting a num- ber of gentlemen out of a scrape. But the epidemic was not the reason of the compromise: The real cause of the
compact which the Tories and Liberals had arrived e, was to be found in another direction. The reason was that .the Liberal party had suddenly . . . .

become aware of the object of the Meeting which they were holding that night ; and had further become cog- nizant of the fact, that had they entered upon a contest they would have emerged *from in a more battered state than when they entered. The Liberal party had evidently intended to make a contest, because even on the previous day they were hunting all over the town for candidates, and had invited their humble servant (the chairman) to " come out." But he was not going to stand up for the Liberal party, to receive another "knock-down blow." (Laughter.) The speaker next proceeded to criticise the Liberal party. He said his object in doing so was to brill.. some of the party leaders to their senses. It was not bring show any ill :Poling between the Irish community of the town and the Liberal community ; tut it was simply to show the rank and file of tite Liberal party, that one or two of their !eaders were bringing the party name into ill. repute by their mean and dispicable actions. (Hear, hear.) Since 1886 he had understood that an alliance had existed between the Liberal party and the Irish party on an understanding based upon the Home Rule question. It had been his impression, and the impres- sion of his fellow-countrymen that the alliance was founded upon the principles of justice and equality. They thought it was a compact entered upon by honourable and honest men. But it was not; and he . .

was sorry to say that the Liberal leaders of Warrington did not act their part in that compact. Such an alliance, therefore, was bound sooner or Ater to end. They would remember that two years ago there was going to be a contest in St. John's Ward,and the Irishmen of the town, on the strength of this alliance, and thinking they would be fairly dealt with by the Liberal party,claimed to have a representative in the Town Council. He (Mr. Lough- lin) was unanimously elected to fight the battle. How- ever, within 24 hours of this decision the wirepullers of the Liberal Party appointed a deputation of three to writ upon a certain gentleman who was reported to have influence with him (Mr. Loughlin), and ask him to advise him (Mr. Loughlin) to with- draw from the contest. The gentleman, however, refused to do such a mean, contemptible despic- able piece of work. (Applause.) Finding they could ' not effect their purpose, the Liberal Party determined to make the best of a bad job. A certain alderman of the town was asked to nominate him, but he hesitated to do so, and said that he would require a certificate of loyalty to the effect that he did not intend to dismember the British Empire. (Laughter.) After this he felt inclined to withdraw from the contest, but he was then obliged to go on. The ward was canvassed and re-can- vassed. The result was ancient history. He was ignominiously defeated in a thoroughly Liberal Ward— the most Liberal ward in the Borough. He believed the reason was ti- he was an Irishman. After this the Irian party of the town were not satisfied, because they felt they had i t been treated in a proper manner, and it went without saying that he was defeated by Liberal vo .es. It was clearly proved that his defeat was brought at rut by so-called Liberals, who, because an Irishman stood before them, became Tories at once. In the last elections the Irish party determined not to work for the Liberal candidates, and the Liberals then became alarmed. The: began a series of visits to his (Mr. Loughlin's) shop, and it was no exaggeration to say that at one period there were as many as four or five Liberal leaders at a time there. They tiled by every means to break the resolution of the Irish party, but without avail. At length, Mr. Henry Roberts asked the Irish party to meet the leaders of the Liberal party, and it was consented to do this. The meeting was held in that very hall on the 26th Octobers Among the Liberal leaders present were Mr. William Pierpoint, Mr. H. Roberts, Mr. Charles Jackson Holmes, Mr. John Walker, Mr. S. H. Fleming, and others. They (the Irish Party) were asked to state their grievance, and they stated that they wanted to be treatc 1 with perfect equality, and claimed to have representatives in the Town Council. He was bound to say that there was no demur to this, and the Liberal leaders expressed the opinion that it was a very just claim. Mr. Henry Roberts went as far as to say that they were perfectly entitled to what they claimed. They also claimed to contest, at the earliest opportunity, the rafest seat in the posse ;sion of the Liberal party. (Applause.) The jus- tice of this claim was also admitted, and Mr. Henry Roberts produced from his fertile brain a scheme likely , to answer their purpose, if it was honestly intended. 'This scheme was that the exezutive take the matter in hand, and, at an early meeting, pass a resolution to the. . effect that it was just and desirable in the interests of ; the Liberal party in Warrington that, at the earliest possible moment the Nationalist Paity be represented in the Town Council in Warrington, and that this reso- lution go out to the ward committee, who would get the machinery at work to bring about the desired result. There was nothing dishonourable about all this, except the sequel. The initial step was never taker, the remainder of the executive were never told of what had taken place, the terms of the resolution were never sub- mitted to any executive meeting, and, in a word, instead of keeping their promise, the Liberal leaders falsified it in every way. He defied any one to contradict what lie had said. The speaker then went on to say that the Liberal leaders in Warrington detested the Irish party, and lie could not assign any reason for this except that they (the Irish party) voted independently in 1885. He believed that the Liberal party were determined not to forgive the Irish party for their independent action M 1885. He knew for a 'fact that a certain prominent man in the Liberal ranks, who heard of the affair in 1885,! boldly said Well, if they do, twill defranchise the devils." He had always been under the impression that the franchise was in the hands of the Legislature, and not in the hands of private individuals. He considered that the Irish party had been treated in a shameful manner by the Liberals. He could say unhesitatingly that almost all the prominent Liberals in the town owed their positions to the hard work and loyalty of the Irish community. He would conclude by stating that if the Liberal party thought that they could afford to ignore the Irish party, they were mistaken. If they took up such a course their (the Liberal) party, which was already going to smash, would receive its ultimate end. Finacially the Liberals were rotten. He knew that several prominent men el the party had had to pledge their names at the bank for the support of the organisation. Mr. MULLIN said the Catholic electors comprised one- sixth of the population of the borough. and where, lie asked, was there an office in the Corporation which was held by one of their number? Next November they would take care there was an election. They would put a man up and force an election. The Irish party and the Labour party weuld unite to force the hands of the Liberals.

Mr. DONELIAN also addressed the meeting, and pressed the claims of the Irish electors. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Kiernan had been asked to preside, but he was unavoidably detained. The speaker said that four or five gentlemen put their heads tog,ether and decided to present a testimonial to the doctor. They sent circulars out to those persons who they thought would subscribe; but the miserable, paltry sum that was collected, if it was divided amongst the Liberals of Warrington, would not amount to a penny apiece. They then decided to hold a meeting, he supposed, without the. consent of Dr. Houston' to make the pre- sentation. Dr. Houston evidently heard of this and decided not to come near the town. So a few of the gentlemen whose names were on the subscription lis', then went to Dr. Houston, at Chester, were they made the presentation. They wanted to see a decent 'Liberal party. He was convinced that Warrington properly worked was a Liberal borough. He attributed the de- feat at the general election to mismanagement, and want of confidence in the rank and file of the party. Mr. J. PRICE said he was glad the treachery, coward- liness, and unmanliness of the Liberal party had been brought forward that night. He thought those who had the management of affairs should move out of the wa v, and make room for better men. ,The Liberal party in Warrington was rotten to thC:^core. (Applause.) The me@tinigitfterwirds terminated. , -
HEAVY FINE ON A HOUSE-OWNEE.

At Bristol Quarter Sessions, the Recorder, Mr. Poole, gave his decision upon an appeal by Mr. George Edward Weare, solicitor, against the decision of the justices, who had sentenced him to three months' imprisonment for being the landlord of a house which was used for dis- orderly purposes. The Recorder varied the sentence,and inflicted a fine of £2O instead of imprisonment.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT IN A NEWSPAPER
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT IN A NEWSPAPER
OFFICE. At the " Glasgow Herald" office, on Thursday, John Connell broke his neck by pulling the wrong chin of a paper hoist, Death was instantaneous.
A WRIT OF EXECUTION AGAINST MR. W. O'BRIEN.
The Queen's Bench, Dublin, on Thursday, issued a writ of execution against Mr. W. O'Brien for £3,000, neing the aniount of the judgment obtained in the libel action Bolton v. O'Brien.
ACCOUCHMENT OF THE DUCHESS OF WESTMINSTER.

On Thursday morning the Duchess of Westminster was safely delivered of a son at Eaton Hall, near Chester. It is stated that the mother and son are doing wall. This is the fourth child born to the Duke of Westminster since his marriage with the duchess.
ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER BY A BOY OF NINE.

A charge of manslaughter was preferred at Colchester on Thursday against Frederick Puxley, aged nine years, of West Mersea. The evidence was that Puxley kicked Arthur Smith, a schoolfellow aged nine, and hit him on the head with a Slate while in the playground. Smith died on Wednesday, after declaring Puxley kicked him intentionally. The boy was remanded.

div.head: STRANGE BEQUEST.
div.p: A STRANGE BEQUEST.

The late Dr. W. F. Cumming,of Edinburgh, bequeated MOO to the Infirmary in that city on condition that the annual income derived from it is applied to the pm. chase of snuff and tobacco for poor patients " who may have been addicted to the use of tobacco in any shape and are known to be in distress from want of it." Tea and sugar may be purchased for those who dislike snuff and tobacco. 4. REMARKABLE REVELATIONS AT PRESTON.
A DISEASED MEAT TRADE.

The Preston Town Council on Thursday discussed and adopted a startling report presented by a Special Com- mittee appointed to inquire into allegations that Preston was the market for the disposal of "stink" or diseased meat. The Committee found that such allegations were true, and recommended the dismissal of the meat inspector. Alderman Hibbert, who moved the adoption , of the report, said the dis^,losures made to the Committee were of a most revolting nature. The witnesses all gave , testimony to the effect that there was an extensive trade in bad meat carried on at Preston. and as to the gross neglect of the sanitary officials in the matter. pr. Dunn said the inquiry had dealt a blow at the fearful death- rate of Preston; and Mr. Thompson, another member, stated that the evidence of the witnesses showed that any vile stuff could be got rid of in the town. It was resolved that the evidence taken by the Committee should be printed and circulated .among the members of the Council,

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

VISIT TO THE CANAL. On the invitation of Lord Egerton of Tatton and the directors of the Ship Canal Compaily, the members of the special Ship Canal Committee of the Salford Corporation visited the canal works on Saturday, journeyed from Pomona on the overland route to Weaver Pool, and thence by boat to Liverpool.

div.head: OLDHAM AND THE CANAL.
div.p: OLDHAM AND THE CANAL.

The Oldham Town Council proposes to lend £250,000 to the Ship Canal undertaking on condition that the Corporation is allowed to appoint a representative on the Board of Directors, and that the loan shall rank pani passu with the three millions lent by the Corporation of Mar
nchester. SALFORD CORPORATION AND THE CANAL.

At special meeting held on Wednesday night the General Purposes Committee of the Salford Corporation resolved to recommend the Council, subject to satisfac- tory arrancements being made, to lend a million pounds to the Idanclie,ater Ship Canal Company to help to secure the completion of the works. The Council will meet shortly to consider the recommendation.

div.head: – MANCFIESTER _CORPORATION AND THE
div.p: THE - MANCFIESTER _CORPORATION AND THE
CANAL.

The Special Ship Canal Committee of the Manchester Corporation have prepared a report for consideration by the Council making certain recommendations with regard to advancing the further capital necessary to complete the undertaking. It has been decided after con- sultation with Mr. Moulton, Q.C., that Parliamentary powers shall be sought by the Corporation for the follow- ing objects :—To enable the Corporation of Manchester to advance £2,000,000, to be secured by the issue to the Corporation of debentures similar to, and on the same terms as, the new debentures issued under the Act of 1891, and ranking pan i passu with them ; to give the Corporation power to appoint five additional directors : to confer on the Corporation suitable voting power at shareholders' meetings in respect of their total advances ; to provide that in case Salford or any other town should obtain in the approaching session Parliamentary power to anticipate in the advances made to the Ship Canal Com- pany they shall be entitled to do so, and to share representation upon the directorate in proport u to their share of the total advances under the Act ~1 1891, and the intended Act, viz., one director for each half million, and to have a corresponding voting power ; and lastly, to give power to the Manchester Corporation, also to take up any unissued first and second deben- tures, if thought desirable. The Manchester Corpora- tion are recommended to promote a separate bill in Parliament to give effect to the recommendations.

- WIDNES MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THH BILIICTORS OF FARNWORTH WARD. LADIES AND GKNTLEMEN, At the request of a number ..)f influential burgesses of the Ward, I beg to offer myself as a candidate for the represent- ation of the ward in the Connell. I have resided all my life in the Ward, and have served you to the best of my ability on the Local Board for a number of years. I strongly object to the introduction of politics int o municipal affairs, and therefore I appear before you as an Independent Candidate and not as the nominee of any political party. If you should honour me by returning me as one of your Members to the Council, I shall endeavour to do my duty in the future as I have done in the past, without fear, favour, or bias. I am, ladies and gentlemen, Your obedient servant. FRANCIS HEYES. Appleton, Oct. 14th, 1892.

BOROUGH OF WIDNES. MUNICIPAL ELECTION, NOVEMBER 1, 1892. TO THE ELECTORS OF VICTORIA WARD. LADIES AND GENTLIIIIIDN, I have been requested by a number of Burgesses in this Ward, to offer myself as a Candidate at the forthcoming Election. I therefore beg to ask at your hands the honour of repre- senting you on the Town Council, and respectfully solicit your support, irrespective of party or politics, believing, as I do, that party questions should not enter into municipal matters. If returned as one of your representatives. It will be my endeavour to study the interest of the Town in general, and this Ward in particular; always having regard to efficiency and economy. I am, ladies and gentlemen, Your obedient servant. FREDERICK NEIL. Ann-street, October. 1892.

Having been requested by a large and representative de- putation to offer ourselves as candidates for Tour it, ffrages at the approaching Municipal Election, we have consented to be Nominated, end place our services at your disposal. Our long residence and business connections in the Town and Simms Cross Ward in particular, will enable us to interest ourselves on your behalf in the Council Chamber and Com- mittees on the social and Sanitary Questions which affect the life and comfort of our large working class population. We are, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servants, JOHN BEECH, • ROBERT T. HURST, JAMES HOLM%

WIDNES MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO THE ELECTORS OF SIMMS CROSS WARD. LIDIIS AND ENT LIM EN, Having been requested to become a Candidate at the ensu- ing Municipal Election. I have decided to accede to the same on INDEPENDENT LINES. As a native of the good old town, it Is my highest ambition to become a member of its first Council. A. a member of the Local Board, I trust my conduct will have met with your approval. As a non-party man, but as one who has always tried to do his duty irrespective of PARTY or POLITICS, I appeal to you for your vote and confidence, assuring you nothing shall be wanting on my part to further the interests of our Borough, and of dIMMS CROSS WARD in particular. lam, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, GEORGE INGRAM NELL. Simms Cross, October 7th, 1892.

BOROUGH OF WIDNES. MUNICIPAL ELECTION, NOVEMBER 1. TO THE ELECTORS OF VICTORIA WARD. Linrne awn GE_VTLEMBN, Having been waited upon by two large and influmfilal Deputations of this Ward, I have allowed myself to be nominated as & Candidate. I was born in the Town, and have Resided with you all my Lite. and have learned by practical knowledge its requirements. Moreover, I am • large Property Owner in this and other Wards, and conse- quently have a considerable Stake in the Town and its Welfare ; and may fairly claim to have added somewhat to the Prospetity of the Town by placing my whole Investments in it lam in favour of ;riving all Corporation Contracts to Local Contractors. I need scarce remind the working men of the Ward, that I have shown my sympathy with them in my endeasour to ameliorate their condition, by practical help whenever the opportunity to give it has arisen; and if they show their confidence in me by returning me. my earnest vesolve shall be to serve them to the utmost of my power. Regarding the Sanitary and Financial arrangements of the 'Sown, I consider there is great room for improvemeerst. One Instance will suffice ; let old men sweep the streets instead of the machine brush ; 'this would give these poor people em- ployment, when they could no longer compete with younger men for a living in their respective trades ; and thus save them the degradation of the Workhouse, or beceming a bur- den to the Ratepayers. The streets would be brushed as elven, and, everything considered, it would be equally as economical. HopingTeu will give me yoar hearty support, lam, Ladies arid Gentlemen, Your obedient servant. THOS. HERRAR D. Victoria-road, October, 11392.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. "CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 AND 18136." GLANDERS OR PARcY. NOTICE is Hereby Given, that at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of the County of Chester.held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on Friday, the 21st day of October, 1892., IT WAS ORDERED that the following Regulations, made pursu- ant to Articles 12 and 13 of the Glanders or Farcy Order, 1802, shall, on and after the 24th day of October instant, come into operation, and take effect within the District, under the jurisdiction of this Local Authority, until otherwise modified or revoked. REGULATIONS AS TO MOVEMENT OF HORSES, ASSES, OR MULES, FOR GLANDERS OR FARCY. 1. Any Horse, Ass, or Mule diseased or suspected of Glanders or Farcy, shall not be removed from the stable, building, field, or other place in which it was found to be diseased, or suspected of being diseased, without a Licence of an Inspector of the Local Authority; provided, nevertheless, that such horse, ass, or mule may, for the purpose of being isolated, be removed previous to the case being reported to the Police from any stsch stable, building, field, or other place, to any other building on the same ! premises. 2. That no Horse' Ass, or Rule which has been in con- tact with any diseased or suspected horse, ass, or mule, or which has been otherwise exposed to the imection of Glanders or Farcy, shall be removed from the stable, 'building, field, or other place in which such disease exists, or in which such horse, I ass, or mule has been in contact with any (Ifs- ' eased or suspected horse, ass, or mule, or been otherwise .exposed to the infection of Glanders or Fancy; provided, nevertheless, that this Rulation shall operate so long only as any horse, ass, or mule which in the judgmeat of the Local Authority is diseased, remains in the stable, building, field, or other place, to which the Regulation .refers, and in case ot a stable, hutilding, or other like;plcce,until the Regulations of the Local Authority seas cleansing and disinfection have been Lompiied with by the owner or occupier of such presraises. 3. Thatall fodder, litter, or other thing, that has been in contact with, or used for, or about any diseased or suspected horse, ass, or mule, shall not be taken out of any such stable, building, field, or other place, until -such fodder, litter, or other thing, has bee: as far as practicable disinfected. REGULATIONS AS TO CLEANSING AND DIS- INFECTION IN GMALANDER OR FARCY. 1. That any stable, building, or like place used by, and any utensil, mangers, feeding troughs, pens, hurdles or otherthrin,gs, used for or about any diseased or suspected horse, ass, or Mule, or any van, cart, or ot lierwehicle. used for carrying any diseased or staapectrdo6orse, ass, or male, on land otherwise titan on a.railway, shall he eleanetosi and disinfected at the es,Tensc of the owner, lessee, or occupier tbereof,in the following manner By thoroughly cleansing same by washing with boil- ing water, or by thoroughly scauhlbing and disinfect. ing with a solution of crude carbolic acid in soap and water of the folio'. lug 'proportions, viz.:— Half a plat of acid; mixed with two gallons .of water. THE DARKEST ENGLAND SCHEME. -- DONATION OF £5OO. It is announced that Mr. R. Cory, has given £5OO to " General "Booth by war of encouragement to him in connection with the Darkest England scheme. THE NEW JUDGE AND THE SE SSIONS BAR. It is stated that the members of the bar of the City Sessions, now sitting in St. George's-hall, have for- warded to Mr. Justice Kennedy a telegram congratulat- ing him on his appointment to a judgeship. MURDER OF A DOCIOR. EIGHT NEGROES CONVICTED. CHA.,LESTOWN, MARILAND, Friday.—The murder of Dr. Hill, which in April last nearly caused a bloody race war in this section, resulted yesterday in the convic- tion of eight negroe.s on charges of murder and being accessory to the murder.

• A RUNAWAY HORSE. SEVERAL PERSONS INJURED. A runaway horse dashed into a crowd of people at the Ballast Fruit Market, yesterday. A perfect panic ensued, and before the frightened animal could be cap- tured over a score of persona had been knocked down and injured, two of them so seriously that they had to be removed in an ambulance wagon to the Royal Hospital. Slight hopes of their recovery are entertained.
